en: *The Meaning of the Two Truths*, Scroll One, composed by Hu Jizang.
Master Rui’s Preface to the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* states: "The *Śata-śāstra* governs the external to restrain heterodoxy; this text [the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*] removes [delusions] within."
Due to its lingering influence,
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* is profound and vast,
while the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra* is subtle and penetrating.
If one investigates these four treatises, they are truly like the sun and moon held within one's breast; there is nothing that is not illuminated and clearly perceived.
If one masters these four treatises, [one will attain such clarity].
Then the Buddha-dharma can be clarified.
The Master said:
"Although these four treatises differ in their names and schools,"
To summarize its essential point:
both serve to clarify the two truths and manifest the Way of non-duality.
If one understands these two truths...
If one clearly understands the two truths, then the four treatises will be brilliantly comprehended;
if one does not understand the two truths,
then the four treatises will remain obscure.
For this reason, one must understand the two truths. If one understands the two truths,
[one will not fall into error].
It is not only the four treatises that can clarify this;
all the various sutras also provide full understanding. How do we know this is so?
Therefore, the treatise states:
"The Buddhas always rely upon the two truths when teaching the Dharma.
Since this is so for all Buddhas of the ten directions, [it applies here as well].
One always relies on the two truths to expound the Dharma;
therefore, no sūtra ever departs from the two truths.
Since no sūtra ever departs from the two truths, [the teaching is complete].
If the two truths are clearly understood, all the various scriptures will be comprehended.
Now, although all four treatises contain references to the two truths,
I shall for now examine them according to the text of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*.
The treatise states:
"The Buddhas preach the Dharma for sentient beings by relying on the two truths:
first, the conventional truth."
Second is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
However, when the Master was approaching his passing,
he ascended the high seat and entrusted [the teachings] to his disciples.
Since I left the mountains,
I have taken the two truths as the correct path,
explaining the two truths in more than twenty different ways.
Either in a dispersed or a bound form;
either with chapters and sections divided or undivided;
or opened into three parts.
It is initially composed of ten layers.
The reason it consists of ten layers is precisely to counter the doctrine of the Two Truths held by Dharma Master Kaishan.
The meaning of those two truths consists of ten layers;
in order to address those ten layers, ten layers are elucidated,
with each layer being analyzed and rectified in turn.
The Master spoke only of this meaning, which has multiple layers;
all other meanings were left entirely unexpounded.
As for the existence of multiple versions,
this is not the teaching of Master Xinghuang.
Regarding the ten versions:
The first [section] concerns the general meaning of the two truths;
the last concerns the similarities and differences between the two truths.
Now, the first [section] clarifies the general meaning of the two truths.
However, when the Master explains the meaning of the two truths,
he mostly relies on two sources:
first, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
Second, regarding the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*.
For now, we shall rely on the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* to clarify the meaning of the two truths (*satyadvaya*).
As for why we rely on the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* to discuss the two truths:
The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* takes the two truths as its fundamental tenet.
If one thoroughly understands the two truths,
the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* will then become clear.
For this reason, the Two Truths are explained based on the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*.
The "Chapter on the Four Truths" in the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* states:
"The Buddhas rely upon two truths to teach the Dharma to sentient beings"—
this statement is indeed difficult to understand.
If one asks whether the Dharma is taught based on the two truths,
the explanation is that the two truths are the foundation.
The teaching of the Dharma is the derivative;
the two truths are that upon which it relies.
The teaching of the Dharma is that which relies [upon them].
However, these words are startling;
they are not what has been known from the past. One asks:
how is it known that all Buddhas teach the Dharma by relying on the two truths, and that these two truths are the basis upon which they rely?
The commentary states that this is extracted from the treatise;
it does not rely on human interpretation,
and thus it says:
Because this sutra possesses a treatise (*śāstra*), its meaning is easily understood.
Now, I shall explain it based on that treatise. [This is from] the "Chapter on the Four Truths" (*Catuḥsatya-varga*) of the treatise.
First, the two truths were explained;
next, the teaching of the Dharma based on the two truths was explained.
Regarding the previous explanation of the two truths, it was said:
Regarding conventional truth:
although the nature of all phenomena is empty,
the world, through its inversions, asserts that they exist.
That which is real within the world is called worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The noble ones (*ārya*) truly know that the nature of inversion is emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
To the noble ones, this is reality;
it is called the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Next, it says:
The Buddhas rely upon these two truths to preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
This concludes the preceding explanation of the two truths.
Thereafter, it is clarified that the Buddhas rely upon these two truths to preach the Dharma for sentient beings;
thus, one knows that the two truths are fundamental.
The teaching of the Dharma is the derivative;
the two truths are that upon which it relies.
The teaching of the Dharma is that which relies [upon them].
It is based on these two truths that one preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
Question: It has been said from of old that all Buddhas preach the Dharma based on the two truths.
For ordinary beings, one speaks of the conventional;
for sages, one speaks of the ultimate;
for ordinary beings who rely on conditions, one speaks of existence.
It is for the sake of the noble conditions that emptiness is taught;
this is called preaching the Dharma by relying on the two truths.
Since it is said that one preaches the Dharma for sentient beings by relying on the two truths, [it follows that...]

How can it be said that one teaches existence for the sake of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and emptiness for the sake of noble ones (*ārya*), thereby relying on the two truths (*satyadvaya*) to teach the Dharma?
To clarify this now:
as stated above, that which is real for ordinary beings is called conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Emptiness, which is reality for the noble ones, is called the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
It is in reliance upon these two truths that one preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
Furthermore, it is asked:
With what intention do the Buddhas teach the Dharma by relying on the two truths?
The explanation says:
In order to clarify that all that is spoken by the Buddhas of the ten directions is true,
they teach the Dharma by relying on the two truths. What are these?
"Truth" (satya) has the meaning of "reality.
That which is real for ordinary beings is empty for the noble ones.
Both of these are real.
The Buddhas teach the Dharma based on these two realities;
therefore, all that the Buddhas speak is real.
The teachings of the ninety-six types of non-Buddhist outsiders are false and unreal because they do not rely upon the two truths.
Therefore, although [the world] is false and unreal, the Buddhas teach the Dharma by relying on the two truths;
thus, all that they teach is real. Since everything spoken by the Buddhas is real, [the teaching is true].
Therefore, all Buddhas preach the Dharma by relying on the two truths.
Again, he asked:
If one preaches the Dharma based on the two truths,
is all that preaching of the Dharma real?
The explanation says:
O noble ones, the Tathāgata speaks in reliance upon the realization of the emptiness of the nature of all phenomena as it truly is, just as the noble ones have realized it.
That which is spoken by the Buddhas is also real;
this refers to the fact that teaching the Dharma based on the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is real.
For worldly people, things such as jars and garments are real.
Because the Buddhas speak of things such as jars and garments in accordance with worldly convention,
what they say is also real.
As it is said in the *Śata-śāstra*:
When the Buddha enters the city of Śrāvastī,
there is no fault because he conforms to worldly speech;
this teaching of the Dharma is thus based on conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and is real.
Because it is spoken based on those two realities,
the teachings of all Buddhas are entirely real.
As previously stated, "speaking in reliance on the truths of ordinary beings" means speaking the Dharma in reliance on conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
It is said that one teaches the Dharma by relying on the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya);
one teaches the Dharma to sentient beings by relying on the two truths.
These words must not be disregarded.
Now I ask: when the Dharma is taught based on the two truths,
upon which truth does that basis itself rely?
"Is this a gain? Is this a loss?
Is it both a gain and a loss?
He asked these same questions regarding the Truths as well.
However, the Great Master said:
"The truth of reality is loss;
the truth of teaching is gain."
What is meant by "losing the truth regarding the [four] truths"?
It is that what is substantially real for ordinary beings is truly empty for the noble ones.
This emptiness exists as a reality for both ordinary beings and sages;
therefore, it constitutes a fault.
As for those who have attained the truth through verbal instruction:
The Tathāgata’s words of truth and reality are as follows:
based on the conventional, there is existence;
yet there is existence that does not abide in existence.
There is manifestation, yet it does not exist.
Based on the noble ones, there is no teaching and no non-existence;
there is no non-abiding and no non-existence.
The unmanifest (avijñapti) is not non-existent;
this constitutes the duality of existence and non-existence.
The manifest (vijñapti) is neither existent nor non-existent, which is non-duality.
Non-duality and duality, non-duality and duality:
non-duality and duality constitute principle and teaching;
duality and non-duality constitute teaching and principle.
The teaching is that which should be taught;
the principle is that which is expressed by the teaching.
The two—principle and teaching—are non-dual due to their causal conditions.
This is what it means to attain. Yet,
although the teaching of the truths is thus,
even so, it remains difficult to understand.
Why is this? You preach the Dharma by relying on the two truths;
you preach the Dharma in reliance upon the two truths.
Are these all truths of the teaching?
If they were all truths of the teaching,
it would contradict the treatise.
The Treatise says:
"The nature of all phenomena is emptiness;
yet the world, through its inversions, regards them as existent according to conventional truth."
The noble sages truly know that the emptiness of the nature of inversion is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
The Buddhas rely upon these two truths to teach the Dharma.
How could this [emptiness] possibly be merely a conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)?
Now, this single phrase precisely clarifies that the teaching of the Dharma is based upon the two truths.
That which is relied upon is the truth of reality (satyadharma), while the teaching of the Dharma is the truth of the doctrine (deśanāsatya).
Regarding the question of whether the two truths, which serve as the basis, are attained or lost,
the treatise itself provides the judgment.
The treatise states:
The nature of all phenomena is emptiness;
yet the world, through its inversions, claims they exist.
To ordinary beings, this [emptiness] is the truth.
The noble ones truly know that the nature of inversion is empty and unarisen;
for them, this is the truth.
This, then, distinguishes the two truths of the ordinary person and the noble one.
Although ordinary beings and sages are non-dual,
they are dual in their non-duality;
thus there are the truth of ordinary beings and the truth of sages.
The mundane truths are loss;
the noble truths are gain. Why is this?
Since it is said that the nature of all phenomena is empty, yet they are mistakenly perceived as existing,
and that noble sages truly know that the nature of these misconceptions is empty,
we may therefore know [this].
Ordinary truths are lost when noble truths are attained. Why?
Because ordinary truths are erroneous, they are lost.
The Noble Truths are "attained" because they are non-erroneous.
This [passage] thus opens up the distinction between the truths of ordinary beings and the Noble Truths, and between erroneous truths and non-erroneous truths.
Question: If the two truths upon which these depend possess both erroneous and non-erroneous aspects, this cannot be understood.
Why is this? The Buddha speaks based on non-perversion;
how could he speak to sentient beings based on perversion?
If one were to say that both [views] are non-erroneous regarding the truths,
this would contradict the treatise.
The treatise states:
The world’s inversion is called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) of conditioned phenomena;
the true knowledge of the noble ones (*ārya*), that the nature of inversion is empty, is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
It is in reliance upon these two truths [that this is taught].
He preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings;
therefore, it is known that he speaks based on both the inverted and the non-inverted.
If one follows the treatises,
how could the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possibly rely on inverted views when teaching the Dharma?
"Advancing and retreating makes it difficult to understand; this has not yet been explained, and so forth.
Question: Previously, you stated that regarding the two truths, there is both gain and loss in what is relied upon.
Will this not contradict what the Master taught?
The Master said: "To say that both truths are lost is an error.
How can you now judge that there is gain and loss regarding the two truths?
He explained:
Your statement that [the four] truths are all erroneous—
of what context is this speech?
Now, let it be clarified.
Regarding the phrase "losing all truths":
it does not mean that the truths upon which one relies are lost;
rather, it means that [the truths] have been established through receiving the teachings.
This fails with respect to all truths.
Why? Because the Tathāgata taught that conditioned phenomena exist as designations, yet do not exist [in reality].
The teaching of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is intended to indicate that it is not non-existent; the teaching of duality is intended to indicate non-duality.
Upon hearing this, they form the conceptualization of existence and develop understanding.
To hear that there is no action and no liberation,
and to hear that there is action, liberation, and existence—
this is truly called the conventional truth for ordinary beings.
If one hears that there is no non-action, no liberation,
and no non-existence, then both of these two truths— the noble truth of reality and the ultimate truth— are lost.
Question: In what way is it lost?
Explanation: It is as the Tathāgata has taught that conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma) do not exist as [inherently] existent.
By speaking of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one indicates that it is not non-existent;
by speaking of duality, one causes one to realize non-duality.
It is like pointing at the finger so that one may obtain the moon.
Yet sentient beings, hearing that there is abiding and existence,
or hearing that there is non-abiding and non-existence,
cling to the finger while forgetting the moon.
To abide by the principles left behind in the teachings—
is this not a failure? If that were so,
there would then be two kinds of [understanding] regarding the truths.
First, the truth as the basis;
second, the truth regarding delusion concerning the teachings.
Regarding the truth as the basis:
There is gain and there is loss.
To be deluded regarding the teachings on the truths—
both of these are losses.
Taking the truths as the basis is the root;
being deluded regarding the teachings concerning the truths is the branch.
Regarding "taking the truths as the basis is the root":
Furthermore, to discuss this based on a single transformation of Śākyamuni:
even before Śākyamuni appeared in the world, these two truths already existed;
Śākyamuni relied upon these two truths to preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
Why is this? Because there are no teachings of the Buddhas that do not rely upon the two truths;
therefore, from the very first step, they teach in reliance upon the two truths.
One should know that the basis in the truths is the root,
while delusion regarding the teachings concerning the truths is the branch.
Sentient beings receive the Tathāgata’s teaching on the two truths of existence and non-existence;
they form understandings of existence and non-existence and thereby achieve [their respective results].
This refers to the stage of the Truths (satya) occurring later.
Furthermore, there are three distinctions:
namely, the preceding and succeeding, the agent and the object, and the general and the particular.
These shall be explained starting from the latter.
Regarding the general and the specific:
with respect to the truths as the basis, it is general;
with respect to the confusion regarding the teachings concerning the truths, it is specific.
Regarding the universal application of the basis to the truths:
that which is erroneously conceived by the world as existing is, for the world, real; this constitutes conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
The noble sages truly know that the nature of inversion is emptiness as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
These two truths apply universally to all ordinary beings and noble ones,
as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* records that Mañjuśrī asked:
"Within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), does the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) exist?
Within the ultimate truth, does the conventional truth exist?"
If it exists, then there is but a single truth;
if it does not exist, then...
"Is it not that the Tathāgata has spoken falsely?
The Buddha replied,
"The conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is itself the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya)."
Because they follow the capacities of sentient beings, these two are explained through differentiation.
That which is known by worldly people is called the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya);
that which is known by supramundane sages is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
This is precisely how the two types of persons—mundane and supramundane—are distinguished according to the Two Truths;
such is the exact meaning of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*.
That which is mundane and inverted is called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) of the conditioned.
These noble ones truly know that the nature of inversion is emptiness as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); therefore,
these two are common to the truths.
Regarding the statement that confusion concerning the teachings arises from a distinction between the truths:
the Tathāgata taught the two truths of existence and non-existence in order to manifest the path of non-duality.
Those who possess skillful means hear of duality and awaken to non-duality;
they recognize the principle and awaken to the teaching, which is called the truth of the teaching (śāsana-satya).
Those lacking skillful means,
upon hearing the two abodes and the two [truths],
fail to recognize the underlying principle and become confused regarding the teaching; this is called being deluded about the truths.
Regarding the Truths, it is precisely because they lack skillful means that they are distinct.
As for the terms "subject" and "object":
That which relies upon the truths is the transformer;
that which is deluded regarding the truths through the teachings is the one to be transformed.
This is stated for the time being as a partial explanation from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Why is this? The treatise states: "Because all noble ones truly know that the nature of inversion is empty, they are able to manifest transformations.
This is as explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The Sūtra says:
"All conventional truths (saṃvṛti-satya) are,
for the Tathāgata, the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya)."
Because, for the Tathāgata, conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is itself the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
This ultimate truth is that which is capable of transformation;
such is the correct position of the treatise.
Ordinary beings, being subject to inversion, claim that things exist;
the noble ones, however, know only that the nature of this inversion is empty, neither arising nor ceasing.
For the noble ones, this is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
If that is so, one should know that this ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is the truth of the transformer,
while those who are deluded regarding the teaching concerning truth are the objects of transformation.
Although one may achieve perfection through receiving the teachings, even such a sage is ultimately one who has received the teachings.
Because they have received the teachings, they are those who are to be transformed.
As for the terms "before" and "after," they are no different from "beginning" and "end."
The basis for [understanding] the truths is fundamental and precedes;
confusion regarding the teachings on the truths is derivative and follows.
Thus, the initial step is explained as being based upon the truths.
Thereafter, sentient beings receive the teaching:
those with skillful means awaken to the principle and thus establish the truth of the teaching;
those without skillful means fail to recognize the principle and thus establish [only] the [conventional] truth.
Therefore, the preceding and succeeding [passages] differ.
Next, let us further examine a single sentence.
The previous passage stated: "All noble sages truly know that the nature of inversion is emptiness."
To the noble ones, it is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya),
as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
"All worldly truths (saṃvṛti-satya)..."
If, regarding the Tathāgata, that which is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is such that all conventional truths (saṃvṛti-satya) are said to be the ultimate truth for the Tathāgata,
may it also be said that all ultimate truths are conventional truths for ordinary beings?
The commentary states:
This is derived solely from the *Śāstra*.
The *Śāstra* says:
Regarding conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the nature of all phenomena is empty;
yet, due to worldly perversion, people perceive them as existing,
and for such people, these things are considered real.
This is termed "truth. To explain the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*),
the preceding passage cited the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena (*sarva-dharma-svabhāva-śūnyatā*) as its interpretation.
One clearly understands that the nature of all phenomena is emptiness;
yet the world, through its inversions, claims they exist.
To worldly people, this is considered real and is thus called "truth."
It should be known that all ultimate truths (paramārtha-satya) are,
for ordinary beings, conventional truths (saṃvṛti-satya).
As it is said in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*:
"All dharmas are non-existent, yet they exist in this way;
though they exist in this way, they are non-existent."
Thus, that which does not exist for the noble ones exists as the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) from the perspective of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya);
that which does not exist for ordinary beings exists as such [from their perspective].
The ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Question: With what intention are the two truths of the ordinary person and the sage established? Explanation:
[Response: It is said that...
Now, in opening up the two truths of the gain and loss of the ordinary and the sage, it is shown that the sage gains what the ordinary person loses, thereby inducing awakening.
It clarifies: "This is the truth of the ordinary; this is the truth of the sage; this is the inverted truth; and this is the non-inverted truth."
This demonstrates the distinction between the ordinary and the holy,
causing one to abandon the state of the ordinary and study the holy, to discard error and follow non-error.
For this purpose, the two truths of the gain and loss of the ordinary and the holy are established.
How is this known to be so?
It is fully set forth in the sūtras and śāstras.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra says:
Desiring to cause sentient beings to deeply realize the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya),
the Tathāgata proclaims the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
If sentient beings were not to rely upon the conventional truth, they would not awaken to the ultimate truth.
The Tathāgata never speaks of the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) for its own sake;
rather, he teaches the conventional truth so that one may realize the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Furthermore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Without relying on the conventional truth, the ultimate truth cannot be attained."
If one does not attain the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), one cannot attain nirvāṇa.
By teaching the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one enables the attainment of the ultimate truth;
by teaching the ultimate truth, one enables the attainment of nirvāṇa.
Therefore, the two truths are established.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "The Prajñāpāramitā..."
It arises for the sake of a great matter,
namely, to demonstrate what is the path and what is not the path;
that which is not the path is precisely inversion.
This path is itself not inverted.
To show that this path is [actually] not the path,
it causes one to abandon the non-path and follow the path.
It also demonstrates the inverted and the non-inverted,
so as to cause those who have fallen into inversion to rise up and follow the non-inverted; it is for this purpose.
The two truths are opened up to demonstrate gain and loss,
thereby causing one to transform their understanding.
However, there are three major sections in the broad classification of the two truths.
First, the two truths are distinguished based on whether ordinary beings or sages are subject to inversion or non-inversion.
Second, the two truths are distinguished internally among sages themselves.
Third, the two truths are distinguished internally among ordinary beings themselves.
Regarding the determination of the two truths based on ordinary beings and sages:
that which is understood by ordinary beings is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya),
and that which is understood by sages is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Regarding this distinction between ordinary beings and sages:
it is based on whether one realizes the emptiness of nature or does not realize the emptiness of nature that ordinary beings and sages are distinguished.
One who has not yet realized the emptiness of nature is an ordinary being.
If one knows that intrinsic nature is empty, one is a sage.
This is how the two truths are distinguished from this perspective.
Furthermore, within the state of a sage, the two truths are distinguished internally as follows:
The Noble Ones realize that this emptiness is existence and that existence is emptiness;
these two truths are both the Two Truths of the Noble Ones.
Why is this? For example, regarding the Four Noble Truths:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path are all termed "Noble Truths."
The two truths are likewise so.
Both the ultimate and the conventional are noble truths.
Question: Where is this statement made? Explanation:
It is as clarified at the end of the "Chapter on the Four Means of Gathering" (*catuḥsaṃgrahavastu*) in the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
At times, the meaning unfolds through the spirit;
at other times, one must rely on clear textual evidence.
Now, it is necessary that the meaning be made explicit through the text.
That text states:
"If ordinary beings were to know conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya),
they would be stream-enterers (srotāpanna) up to Buddhas."
If that is so, ordinary beings do not know the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya);
only the noble ones (ārya) know these two truths.
Therefore, both of these truths are "noble truths" (āryasatya).
The general judgment is thus.
Within the category of the noble ones (*ārya*), there are furthermore immeasurable varieties,
as stated in the Great Sūtra:
At one time, I was on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa with Maitreya,
discussing conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
The five hundred śrāvakas were neither aware nor cognizant of it.
How much more so regarding the profound ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Discussing it in this light,
the followers of the two vehicles do not understand the two truths.
Only Bodhisattvas know the two truths;
this would then destroy the traditional interpretation.
Why? Because the tradition has always said:
The three vehicles all converge upon the ultimate truth and alike understand the two truths; however,
the noble ones truly understand the two truths.
The wise possess a semblance of understanding the two truths; those of the Hīnayāna have a semblance of understanding through the seven stages of expedient means,
while those of the Mahāyāna have a semblance of understanding through the thirty minds.
In the Hīnayāna, this refers to the stage of *duḥkha-kṣānti* and above;
in the Mahāyāna, it refers to the first bhūmi and above.
At these levels, one possesses the true understanding of the two truths.

The conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is understood as that which universally conditions appearances resembling principles; the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is understood as the four negations and the hundred absences of predication.
All three vehicles alike understand these two truths.
If this refers to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*,
it clarifies that even the five hundred śrāvakas did not understand the two truths;
they did not even understand the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
How much more so for the profound ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*);
therefore, the meaning [of the former] has never been established.
Now, at this time, this meaning can be attained.
Why is this? Because the minds of those of the Two Vehicles involve birth and cessation, as well as annihilation and permanence,
and thus they do not practice the Middle Way.
They do not see the Buddha-nature.
The Middle Way is the fundamental source;
since they do not recognize this source, [they fail to see it].
How could one know the details?
Since one does not perceive the principle,
how could one recognize the teaching?
Why is this? That which exists cannot become non-existent,
and that which is non-existent cannot become existent.
Existence cannot function as non-existence;
non-existence cannot function as existence;
and the two cannot function as anything other than the two.
The non-dual cannot function as two;
it is obstructed both horizontally and vertically.
If one were a Bodhisattva...
The conditioned is the function of emptiness;
emptiness is the function of the conditioned.
Duality is the function of non-duality.
Non-duality functions as duality,
for there is no obstruction between the horizontal and the vertical.
Regarding the discernment of the two truths within the state of ordinary beings:
"All of them are so; it is simply the Two Truths as explained by those who have come before.
That is what he said.
The three provisional designations and the seven realities constitute the mundane truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
The four negations and the hundred non-assertions constitute the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
The three provisional designations cannot be attained apart from the four negations.
The four extremes cannot obtain the three provisional designations;
non-existence cannot obtain existence,
and existence cannot obtain non-existence.
One must not sever what is not to be severed;
one cannot sever what is not severed.
Such are the two truths.
These are all the two truths of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). How is this known?
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "Sentient beings give rise to views in two ways."
The first is the view of eternalism, and the second is the view of annihilationism.
These encompass both the two views of existence and non-existence, as well as permanence and annihilation.
Furthermore, there is that which takes what is actually mundane to be the ultimate truth.
Furthermore, emptiness is also a truth for ordinary people;
because this emptiness truly exists, emptiness is a truth.
Thus, for ordinary people as well, there are two truths.
This, then, opens up three kinds of two truths;
those who have followed conventional [understanding] of the two truths will inevitably fall into the two truths of ordinary beings.
Why is this? I maintain three types of the two truths.
The first is the distinction between the two truths made by ordinary beings and sages.
Second, distinguishing the two truths from the perspective of the noble ones themselves.
Third, distinguishing the two truths from the perspective of ordinary beings.
Regarding the two truths for ordinary beings:
The three provisional designations constitute the conventional truth for ordinary people;
the four cessations constitute the ultimate truth for ordinary people.
What, then, is your own position?
According to your doctrine, the three provisional designations constitute conventional truth,
while the four negations constitute ultimate truth; thus,
you yourself fall into the duality of the two truths held by ordinary people.
This is not for the sake of providing a comfortable dwelling.
It is like the principle of a single household managing both internal and external affairs;
your formulation of the argument naturally falls outside my own reasoning.
The treatise states: "The Buddhas rely upon the two truths to preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
Having briefly explained the reliance upon the two truths above, we shall next explain how they rely upon the two truths to preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
Question: Since it has been stated that the Dharma is taught in reliance upon the two truths, for whom was it taught and what kind of Dharma was it?
The assembly of people, having received the Great Master’s words, said:
For ordinary beings, he teaches the existence of phenomena;
for noble ones, he teaches the emptiness of phenomena;
for both ordinary beings and noble ones, he teaches the two truths of emptiness and existence.
It is said that the Dharma is taught based on the two truths.
Question: Does the Master have such a statement?
Answer: Indeed, the Master truly has this statement.
However, there are instances where people merely encounter these words and understand only the words themselves, failing to grasp their underlying meaning. Why is this so?
To speak of existence for the sake of ordinary beings,
and to speak of emptiness for the sake of the noble ones—
this is called teaching the Dharma to sentient beings based upon the two truths.
What kind of teaching is this?
The Buddhas preach the Dharma for sentient beings by relying on the two truths.
How can it be said that they teach existence for ordinary beings and emptiness for noble ones?
Is it that the Buddhas rely upon the two truths to teach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings?
Furthermore, do they rely on the conventional truth to speak of existence and then speak of existence for the sake of ordinary people,
and rely on the ultimate truth to speak of emptiness and then speak of emptiness for the sake of the noble ones?
The treatise states:
"The various noble ones truly know that the nature of inversion is emptiness.
Having realized that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty,"
Why then is emptiness further explained?
What is clarified here is as explained in the treatise.
The treatise states: "The Buddhas, relying upon the two truths, preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings."
The Master said: "I preach the Dharma for sentient beings based upon the two truths.
When did I ever say that I preach for the sake of the noble ones?
I preach the Dharma for the sake of ordinary, mundane sentient beings."
The Dharma is not preached for the sake of sages.
Question: On what basis is it determined that the Two Truths are taught for the sake of sentient beings?
Explanation: [As follows:]
This is a judgment, based on the subject-object relationship of delusion and awakening,
as to whether something is taught or not;
it clarifies that sentient beings are deluded regarding existence and non-existence because they have not yet awakened to existence and non-existence.
For the sake of sentient beings, he speaks of existence and non-existence;
he clarifies that "this is existent" and "this is non-existent," that "this is ordinary" and "this is noble," that "this is inverted" and "this is non-inverted.
He causes sentient beings to enter non-existence from existence, and to abandon the ordinary to take up the noble.
It is for this purpose that the two truths are taught.
If they have already been realized by the noble ones,
why would it be necessary to teach them?
Because ordinary beings have not yet attained awakening,
it is necessary to explain the two truths for them;
because ordinary beings have not yet attained awakening, they receive the teachings.
Because the Sage has already attained awakening, he does not rely upon instruction.
As for what is called "subject and object," it refers to all conventional truths (saṃvṛti-satya).
If everything regarding the Tathāgata is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya),
and since everything regarding the Tathāgata is the ultimate truth, he is the transformer;
how could that which is transformed be the transformer who preaches the Dharma?
That which is the ultimate truth for all is,
for sentient beings, conventional truth;
this is because sentient beings are those who are to be transformed.
One must preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.

Next, I shall explain this meaning by means of two passages: one from the "Examination of Phenomena" (*Dharmaparīkṣā*) chapter of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* and another from the commentary on the "Rebirth" (*Upapatti*) chapter of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, in the "Examination of Dharmas" chapter,
states: "The Buddhas sometimes speak of a self,
and sometimes they speak of non-self."
Within the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena,
there is neither self nor non-self;
this is explained in the prose section.
I teach non-self for the sake of ordinary beings,
and I also teach non-self for the sake of noble ones who have attained the Path.
Self and non-self are thus the two truths.
Therefore, the first chapter of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Beings such as humans exist according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*),
but they do not exist according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)."
You should know that "self" is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya),
while "non-self" is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Since one speaks of self and non-self for ordinary beings,
and speaks of self and non-self for noble ones,
one thereby speaks of the two truths for ordinary beings.
This is for the sake of explaining the two truths to the noble ones.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, in its commentary on the "Chapter on Rebirth," states:
Question: [As follows].
In the preceding "Chapter on Practice and Response," it was clarified that if there were no bodhisattvas, there would be no coming or going. Why, then,
is it now said that there are bodhisattvas and that there is coming and going?
The commentary states:
There is no contradiction;
it is for the sake of ordinary beings that [the Buddha] taught there is no coming or going.
Is it for the sake of the noble ones that coming and going are said to exist? Is it for the sake of the noble ones that coming and going are said not to exist?
Or is it for the sake of ordinary beings that coming and going are said to exist?
However, since the past and future lack coming and going, these are still the two truths.
Are these two truths taught for ordinary beings,
or are they taught for the noble ones?
The general meaning is the same as that of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*.

However, the Master further clarifies that he teaches existence for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and emptiness for noble ones (*ārya*), and that he teaches both emptiness and existence for both ordinary beings and noble ones.
These constitute three sections that explain the meaning of the two truths (*satyadvaya*).
The two truths were previously explained for the sake of ordinary beings;
they are not explained as two truths for the sake of noble ones.
Furthermore, the distinction between delusion and awakening, and between subject and object, is to be judged as before.
Next, the *Dharmapada* is explained.
Question: With what intention was the *Dharmapada* taught—was it for the sake of ordinary beings that the two truths were taught, or for the sake of noble ones?
The commentary states:
For the sake of ordinary beings, one speaks of self and non-self;
just as previously for ordinary beings one spoke of existence and non-existence to lead them toward awakening to neither existence nor non-existence.
The self and the non-self are likewise so.
Sentient beings are deluded regarding the self and the non-self;
for their sake, I speak of the self and I speak of the non-self.
It causes one to be free from both self and non-self.
To be free from self is to be free from permanence;
to be free from non-self is to be free from annihilation.
This is because it causes them to abandon the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism and realize the Middle Way.
For ordinary beings, one speaks of both self and non-self;
for noble ones, one likewise speaks of both self and non-self.
The Sage understands both self and non-self;
therefore, he teaches self and non-self for the sake of the Sage.
Previously, he taught self and non-self for the sake of ordinary beings.
Ordinary people are deluded regarding self and non-self;
for the sake of the sages, one speaks of self and non-self.
It is not that the sages are deluded regarding self and non-self, and thus [the teaching] is spoken for their sake.
However, because the sages understand "self" and "non-self" upon hearing them,
they teach "self" and "non-self" for that very purpose.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* cites the *Devaparipṛcchā-sūtra*, stating:
"Can an Arhat in his final body say 'self' or 'no-self'?
The commentary explains:
Because it can be explained, the Noble Ones understand that "I" is non-self (*anātman*).
Furthermore, it is said:
"It is like a military secret code; only those on guard understand it, while others do not."
When it is said that there is a self and no-self,
only the noble ones understand this; others do not understand it.
Because the Noble Ones are able to understand "self" and "non-self," they teach "self" and "non-self" for the sake of the Noble Ones.
This is also the case in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*.
The categories of those who attain rebirth can be known accordingly.
Question: Ordinary beings are deluded regarding self and non-self;
for the sake of ordinary beings, you speak of self and non-self.
Causing one to realize "self" and "non-self" can be beneficial;
the noble ones understand self and non-self.
"What benefit is there in speaking for the sake of sages?
The commentary explains:
"This is not spoken with reference to benefit."
It is directly evident that ordinary beings do not understand "self" and "non-self," whereas the noble ones understand "self" and "non-self.
Because the noble ones understand "self" and "non-self," [the Buddha] speaks of "self" and "non-self" for the sake of the noble ones.
This is for the benefit of ordinary beings;
it benefits others rather than oneself.
It is as Ānanda stated: "Thus have I heard."
This is for the benefit of sentient beings.
Next, the Great Master said:
"For ordinary beings, one speaks of existence; for sages, one speaks of emptiness."
These ordinary beings and sages are the objects of transformation;
among the ordinary beings and sages who receive the teachings,
there are those who are truly ordinary.
For the sake of ordinary beings, one speaks of existence to lead them to realize non-existence;
emptiness is the reality for the noble ones.
For the sake of the noble ones, one speaks of emptiness to lead them to realize non-emptiness.
It causes ordinary beings and sages to speak of existence and non-existence while awakening to the fact that there is neither existence nor non-existence;
it also causes ordinary beings to awaken to what is not ordinary,
and causes sages to awaken to what is not sage-like.
It is the Middle Way of the True Dharma, neither ordinary nor holy;
therefore it is said:
"It is not the practice of an ordinary person."
This is not the practice of the noble ones; it is the practice of bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, that which is taught as conditioned for ordinary beings is taught as empty for the noble ones.
It is explained according to ordinary beings that [form] exists, and according to noble ones that it does not exist,
just as with a single form which exists for ordinary beings but does not exist for noble ones; thus, it is explained according to ordinary beings that form exists.
When it is said that form does not exist according to the teaching of the Noble Ones, it is not that form has never existed at all;
this is specifically intended as a refutation of the views held by those who have come from elsewhere.
He said: "The three provisional designations constitute the principle of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya);
the fourfold transcendence constitutes the principle of ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya)."
There are two truths; the principle is now clarified:
according to the perspective of ordinary beings, existence is taught.

To say that [the two truths] do not exist in accordance with the noble ones is merely to say that existence and non-existence are taught in accordance with both ordinary beings and the noble ones. Where,
then, is there any principle of two truths?
For this reason, it is said that existence and non-existence are taught for the sake of ordinary beings and sages.
This concludes the explanation regarding sentient beings.
Next, the exposition of the teaching is explained.
Generally, there are three types of teaching:
some fully expound the two truths.
Some speak only of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) and not of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya);
others speak only of conventional truth and not of the ultimate truth.
These three types all appear in the sūtras and śāstras.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, in its commentary on the "Chapter on Rebirth," states:
Question: This was previously discussed in the "Chapter on Practice."
This clarifies that when a bodhisattva practices in accordance with prajñā,
they do not perceive a bodhisattva,
nor do they perceive prajñā.
"If there is no bodhisattva and no prajñā,
for what purpose do you now further say that there are bodhisattvas who pass away from this life and are reborn in another?
He replied:
Previously, it was explained that there is no bodhisattva and no prajñā from the perspective of the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya).
Now, it is explained that bodhisattvas are reborn [in the Pure Land].
This explains *prajñā* by way of the gate of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
This is thus an explanation of *prajñā* by means of the two truths.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"Good son, do not enter the profound samādhi of emptiness.
Why is this? Because the great assembly is dull-witted."
This should be explained by means of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
This also explains, in terms of the two truths, the meaning of "not hearing what is heard" regarding nirvāṇa.
As previously stated, one should not enter the profound concentration of emptiness because the assembly is dull-witted.
This is spoken from the perspective of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya);
it should now be explained by means of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
This, then, is spoken from the perspective of conventional truth.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Because he wishes to expound the ultimate *siddhānta*, he teaches the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*;
this, then, speaks exclusively of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)."
Furthermore, the Mahāyāna Sūtra states that when discussing conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) with Maitreya, five hundred śrāvakas were neither aware nor cognizant of it;
this refers exclusively to conventional truth.
Although these three types are distinct,
that which is taught by the Tathāgata does not transcend the two truths.
Question: With what intention did the Tathāgata teach that the Dharma does not transcend the two truths?
Explanation:
The two truths are precisely the four *siddhāntas*.
The three *siddhāntas* are the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The *paramārtha-siddhānta* is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
The four *siddhāntas* encompass the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*).
It encompasses the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma;
since the encompassing of all dharmas is complete,
the encompassing of all dharmas within the two truths is likewise complete.
This explains the meaning of "exhausting what is inexhaustible.
Since all phenomena are fully encompassed within the two truths,
the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma by means of these two truths.
Question: Since the two truths and the four *siddhāntas* encompass all phenomena exhaustively,
for what purpose do the Buddhas rely upon the two truths when preaching the Dharma?
Is it not taught according to the four *siddhāntas*?
The explanation says:
all [of them] are applicable.
Since it is explained based on the two truths, it is also explained based on the four *siddhāntas*.
Why is it that the particular case cannot be generalized? This is because there is a specific meaning here.
To clarify that all that the Buddhas have spoken is true,
the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* states:
"The Tathāgata is one who speaks truthfully, one who speaks reality."
Therefore, it is based on the two truths that the names of the four *siddhāntas* are taught;
they do not refer to a primary, ultimate reality.
Therefore, it is not based on the four *siddhāntas* that this is taught.
Question: If the teaching of the Dharma is not based on the four *siddhāntas*, what is the purpose of using the four *siddhāntas*?
The commentary states:
The two truths are that upon which one relies;
based on the two truths, one expounds the Dharma of the four *siddhāntas*.
This also consists of two types;
each takes one meaning to clarify it.
To speak of their actual meanings is called the four *siddhāntas*.
The explanation of the actual meaning is termed the two truths;
this is based upon the two truths.
The skillful means belong to different conditions.
Therefore, there are four kinds of *siddhānta*.
Question: How are the four *siddhāntas* explained in reliance upon the two truths?
Explanation: [As follows:]
Based on the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), the ultimate tenet (paramārtha-siddhānta) is taught;
based on the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), the three tenets are taught.
This is taught according to the ultimate truth.
They are joined and do not open;
this is spoken according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
They are opened and do not join.
Because it relies on the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), it explains the ultimate standpoint (paramārtha-siddhānta) and thus remains unified without being opened up; whereas,
relying on conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), it explains the three standpoints (traya-siddhānta).
It is opened but not closed.

Question: What is the meaning behind the fact that, according to the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), it is closed but not opened, whereas according to the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), it is opened but not closed?
The commentary states:
Since there are two truths,
why would one suddenly merge or separate them?
The causes and conditions of the ultimate and the conventional are the causes and conditions for their opening and closing.
Question: Are these not both equally the causes and conditions of the two truths?
Why is it that the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is unified and not differentiated,
while the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is differentiated and not unified?
The explanation says:
In the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), there is both emptiness and existence; in the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), there is existence and emptiness.
This is the ultimate truth.
Difference and non-difference;
in the conventional truth there is neither difference nor non-difference;
in the ultimate truth, duality and non-duality are one.
In the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), non-duality is duality; for this reason,
the conventional truth is opened but not joined.
The ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is unified and not divided.

Question: Regarding the statement that the ultimate standpoint (*paramārtha-siddhānta*) is taught based on the ultimate truth—this refers to the true knowledge of all noble ones (*ārya*) that the nature of all phenomena (*dharma*) is empty.
It is based on that very realization of the emptiness of intrinsic nature that one speaks of all phenomena as being originally unborn and quiescent;
this is intelligible.
If it is asked whether the three *siddhāntas* are taught based on the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the explanation is as follows:
the three *siddhāntas* are all taught because they rely upon the conventional truth.
Phenomena such as jars, clothing,
and vehicles are considered real within the world;
this is termed "worldly truth" (saṃvṛti-satya).
Based on worldly convention, the world-siddhānta is taught;
for example, it is said that the combination of the hub, spokes, and rim constitutes a chariot,
and the combination of the five aggregates constitutes a person.
To speak in this manner is the world-view standpoint (*loka-siddhānta*). Thus,
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
Because of the world of humans and so forth, [things] exist;
in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), they do not exist.
This is what is called the "worldly comprehensive standpoint" (*loka-siddhānta*) as taught according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Regarding the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the therapeutic standpoint) as explained according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*):
sentient beings briefly have the three poisons as their illnesses;
in detail, they have the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*) as their illnesses.
There are eighty-four thousand dharma-medicines of the pāramitās that counteract these illnesses;
this is called the Siddhānta of Counteraction (pratipakṣa-siddhānta).
Why is it called "antidote"?
Because one dispels illness with medicine,
and one treats illness with medicine.
This is called the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of therapeutic remedies). Just as medicine and disease counteract one another,
the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* is taught here based on conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Therefore, the treatise says:
"They exist as antidotes;
in their true nature, they are non-existent."
It should be understood that this is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the tenet of counteracting) taught according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
As for teaching "according to the individual" (*pratyātma-vinaya*) based on conventional truth:
The previous explanation of the three dharma-medicines— the eighty-four thousand pāramitās—
curing the three poisons and the eighty-four thousand afflictions,
clarifies that all dharmas are thus exhausted.
What further could be discussed?
The explanation says:
among those who act as individuals.
Furthermore, consider this:
for what reason do the sūtras of the Buddhas sometimes speak of a self and sometimes speak of non-self?
At one time you speak of permanence;
at another moment you speak of impermanence.
For what reason do you sometimes speak of Vairocana and sometimes speak of Śākyamuni?
Some say it is pure, while others say it is impure.
Why are these preceding and succeeding statements mutually contradictory?
For this reason, the *puruṣapudgalasiddhānta* (the standpoint established for specific individuals) is explained next.
In the past, because they were attached to what is impermanent, I taught impermanence;
this was to clarify that even Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas relinquish their impermanent bodies.
Now, because people are attached to the three types of cultivation and to worldly honors, I teach permanence.
In the past, because their faculties were dull, I taught three [vehicles].
Now, because they are attached to those three, I teach one.
For the sake of those with great faculties as a condition, I teach this Śamatha.
The statement that this is Śākyamuni is made for the sake of those of the Hīnayāna;
such cases are all due to differences in the specific circumstances [of the teaching],
and there is no contradiction.
This refers to the teaching of the three *siddhāntas* based on the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
As for the teaching of the *paramārtha-siddhānta* based on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*),
it subsumes the preceding three.
It is clear that there is no birth and no extinction, no movement and no dependence.
Wherein could there be a person, a vehicle, medicine, illness, a human being, a dharma, permanence, impermanence, a threefold world, or a single self?
Thus, ultimate purity is called the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate standpoint). For this reason,
it is said that the four *siddhāntas* are taught in reliance upon the two truths.
This concludes the explanation of the four *siddhānta* teachings based on the two truths.
Next, we shall clarify the teaching of the Dharma by means of the two truths, relying upon the two truths themselves.
Indeed, the four *siddhāntas* are nothing other than these two truths.
It is merely that their combination and separation constitute difference.
Separating the two truths results in the four *siddhāntas*;
combining the four *siddhāntas* results in the two truths.
The true meaning of the four *siddhāntas* is called the two truths;
the ultimate meaning of the two truths is called the four *siddhāntas*.
To teach the Dharma by means of the gateway of the two truths:
There are three meanings to this:
first, it explains the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya),
so as to cause sentient beings to realize the ultimate truth.
Second, by teaching the two truths, one causes them to leave behind the two views of existence and non-existence.
Third, by teaching existence and non-existence, one causes them to realize that which is neither existent nor non-existent;
this is teaching duality so as to awaken to non-duality.
Regarding the teaching of the two truths to bring about the realization of the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*): as was initially analyzed,
worldly delusion consists in asserting that all phenomena (*dharmas*) exist.
In the world, that which is real is called a truth (*satya*).
The noble ones (*ārya*) truly know that its nature is inverted emptiness (*viparyāsa-śūnyatā*).
For the noble ones, this is reality;
it is termed "truth" (*satya*).
This, then, opens up the two truths of gain and loss pertaining to ordinary beings and noble ones.
It causes sentient beings to realize the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya):
that ordinary worldly people, through their inversions, claim things exist,
whereas the noble ones truly know that the nature of these inversions is emptiness.
It causes one to abandon existence and enter emptiness, transforming the ordinary person into a sage, relinquishing error for attainment.
That sentient beings transform from the ordinary into the sagely is because they awaken to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
If one does not awaken to the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya),
one cannot transform the ordinary into the holy, nor abandon loss for gain;
this is truly because of awakening to the ultimate truth.
It is precisely because one can thus transform the mundane into the sacred and abandon loss for gain that the two truths—
the ultimate and the conventional,
the mundane and the sacred, and loss and gain— are opened up for this purpose.
This is to cause one to awaken to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Regarding the teaching of the two truths to bring about detachment from the two views of existence and non-existence,
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
The Bodhisattva dwells in the two truths and preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
The commentary explains:
For sentient beings who cling to the view of existence,
he teaches the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya);
for sentient beings who cling to the view of non-existence, he teaches the conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya).
For the sake of sentient beings who cling to the dualistic views of existence and non-existence,
the Bodhisattva dwells in the two truths and expounds the Dharma.
Master Zhao’s treatise is likewise so.
Borrowing existence to emerge from non-existence;
borrowing non-existence to emerge from existence;
borrowing existence to emerge from non-existence.
Abiding in conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), one refutes the view of non-existence;
by borrowing non-existence, one emerges from existence.
Abiding in ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), one refutes the view of existence.
Therefore, it is said that the two truths are taught to refute the two views.
Teaching the two truths so as to lead to the realization of non-duality is,
for example, as explained in the *Avataṃsaka*, where one clearly understands that all phenomena, whether existent or non-existent, are neither existent nor non-existent.
This explains that there is awakening to neither existence nor non-existence;
it explains that through the two, one awakens to the non-dual.
This is the meaning of both principle and teaching.
In all sutras and treatises,
whatever has been taught does not go beyond these three kinds.
However, the two truths previously explained were intended to lead one to realize the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
These two truths involve both gain and loss;
for the nature of all phenomena is emptiness.
What is called "inverted" refers to the existence of dharmas as truths;
this is precisely the loss of truth.
All noble ones truly know that the nature of phenomena is emptiness.
This is precisely the attainment of the truths;
therefore, these two truths involve both gain and loss.
Next, the teaching of the two truths is intended to cause one to leave behind the two views.
Both of these truths are erroneous.
Why? Because one would be teaching the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) for the sake of those who cling to the existence of sentient beings.
For the sake of sentient beings who are attached to emptiness, the conventional truth is taught.
Both this existence and non-existence are objects of attachment for sentient beings;
therefore, they lose [the truth] in both cases.
Next, the non-duality of these two awakenings is explained.
Both of these truths are attained. Why is this so?
By means of the two, one awakens to the non-dual.
The "two" refers to principle and teaching;
the "non-dual" refers to teaching and principle.
Duality is precisely the middle and the provisional;
non-duality is precisely the provisional and the middle.
Duality is precisely essence and function.
Non-duality is the very essence of function;
therefore, these two truths constitute attainment.
Next, the aforementioned two truths are designated as the mundane truth and the noble truth.
The conventional truth is the truth of ordinary beings;
the emptiness of intrinsic nature is the truth of the noble ones.
This is the second pair of truths.
All of these are mundane truths.
For those who cling to the existence of sentient beings, one speaks of emptiness;
for those who cling to emptiness, one speaks of existence.
Borrowing existence to refute non-existence, and borrowing non-existence to refute existence—
this existence and non-existence are both the truths of ordinary beings.
Furthermore, there is another meaning of the Noble Truths. What is it?
To rely upon existence or non-existence is a sickness; both are merely mundane.
It is able to borrow both existence and non-existence as medicines; all are sacred.
Third, regarding the Two Truths:
the realization of non-duality through the provisional meaning of the Middle Way.
These two truths are both sacred.
As it is said in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*:
"Phenomena produced through causes and conditions..."
What I teach is emptiness;
it is also a provisional designation,
and it is the meaning of the Middle Way.
It has always been clear that these three are identical in meaning: first,
that causes and conditions are themselves emptiness.
The second is the conventional truth;
the third is the middle [truth]. These two truths—
How could this be known by ordinary beings?
Only the sages can comprehend it;
furthermore, it is beyond the reach of those of the two vehicles.
This is simply the domain of the Bodhisattvas.
Question: For what reason is the Dharma taught by means of the two truths?
What benefit is there in teaching the two truths?
The commentary states:
To provide a brief overview, two passages from the treatises are cited.
First, the "Chapter on the Four Truths" in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* says:
If a person cannot know how to distinguish between the two truths,
they will not understand the clear meaning of reality within the profound Buddha-dharma;
if one does not comprehend the two truths, [one cannot realize the truth].
If one does not understand the two truths, one will not know the true reality of the profound Buddha-dharma;
however, if one realizes the two truths,
one will then know the true meaning of the profound Buddha-dharma.
Therefore, it is known that the teaching of the two truths has great benefit.
Second, the "Chapter on Contemplating Nature" in the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra* states:
If a person does not understand the two truths,
they will not attain self-benefit, benefit for others, or mutual benefit;
if they understand the two truths, they will attain these three benefits.
These two treatises are mutually complementary;
however, these two benefits encompass all possible benefits exhaustively.
The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* clearly elucidates the benefit of the profound Buddha-dharma.
The twelve gates clarify the benefit of enlightening sentient beings;
seeking [enlightenment] above and transforming [beings] below do not go beyond these two benefits.
Question: If one does not understand the two truths, is there no benefit for that person?
Explanation:
Within the Buddha-dharma, even those of the Śrāvaka and Vaipulya vehicles may fail to understand the two truths.
This causes great harm to the Buddha-dharma. Why?
Because the Sārvastivādins and others reckon that all phenomena exist.
Then one does not recognize the Tathāgata’s ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
It is by recognizing the ultimate truth that one becomes a noble one (*ārya*);
since one does not recognize the ultimate truth, [one cannot become so].
This constitutes a refutation of all the noble ones (ārya).
The *Śāstra* states: "The true knowledge that the nature of phenomena is emptiness is called the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya).
Since you do not recognize the ultimate truth, you thereby refute the noble ones."
This is a great error. Next,

there are the followers of the Vaipulya who calculate that all dharmas are empty like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a hare, asserting that there is no causality and no way of ruler and minister, father and son, loyalty and filial piety.
This person does not recognize the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) of the Tathāgata.
If one does not recognize conventional truth,
what fault is there in this?
If one loses the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), one loses the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
If one loses the ultimate truth, one cannot attain nirvana.
As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
If one does not rely on conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), one cannot attain ultimate truth (paramārtha).
If one does not attain ultimate truth, one cannot attain nirvana.
Therefore, this person’s fault is extremely grave.
These two persons encompass all cases exhaustively.
Whether internal or external, great or small, all who maintain the view that things exist share the same fault as the Sautrāntikas.
Regarding all things— large or small, internal or external— that are reckoned as non-existent,
there is no fault in their being equally non-existent according to the Vaipulya (Extensive) teachings.
Furthermore, as it says at the beginning of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*:
Five hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
the faculties of human beings will have become dull;
they will seek the definitive characteristics of the twelve links of dependent origination, the five aggregates, and so forth.
This is precisely a failure to understand the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Upon hearing the Mahāyāna teachings that all things are ultimately empty,
they do not know by what causes and conditions they are empty.
If all things were ultimately empty,
then there would be no such things as sin, merit, or karmic retribution;
this would mean one does not understand conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
For the sake of these sentient beings who hold the two views of existence and non-existence, the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna composed this *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*.
This means that by abiding in the two truths, one refutes the two views of sentient beings.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"The Bodhisattva abides in the two truths."
He preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
What kind of bodhisattva is he?
It is none other than Nāgārjuna himself.
Because sentient beings seek the fixed characteristics of the twelve links of dependent origination and the five aggregates,
and upon subsequently hearing that the Mahāyāna is ultimately empty, they claim there is neither sin nor merit;
such individuals thus lose sight of the two truths.
The Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna composed the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* in order to refute these two [views],
from beginning to end.
One seeks all phenomena and finds them ultimately unobtainable;
thus one abides in the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) and destroys the view of existence.
Next, it further says:
Although it is empty, it is not annihilated;
although it exists, it is not eternal.
Thus, there are the two truths as the gateway of teaching.
When would the Three Jewels, the Four Noble Truths, cause and effect, and sin and merit cease to exist?
This is precisely the refutation of the view of non-existence by abiding in conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Furthermore, what preceded this was the refutation of existence by borrowing emptiness.
The subsequent Chapter on the Four Truths employs existence to refute emptiness,
just as the *Śata-śāstra* employs unity to refute difference and employs difference to refute unity.
The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* is likewise.
These two works each demonstrate a particular perspective.
The former presentation of refutation is followed by a distinct refutation. Regarding the former presentation of refutation:
it refutes the view of emptiness within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) by means of the causal conditions of the Tathāgata.
The first section, "Abiding in the Ultimate Truth of the Tathāgata’s Causes and Conditions," refutes the view of existence;
this is followed by a general refutation, and finally, a specific refutation.
Using existence to refute non-existence,
and using non-existence to refute existence—
this existence and non-existence are both the existence and non-existence of sentient beings.
All must be torn and washed;
not a single thing is to be left behind.
If there is nothing to tear, borrow something that has.
Since existence is negated and non-existence is also eliminated,
this is a thorough refutation.
This explains the refutation of the two views of sentient beings by means of the two truths.
Therefore, there is great benefit.
Next, we shall further clarify how the two previous individuals have lost the meaning of the Two Truths.
This was explained previously.
Sāṃmitīya: [They] claim that all phenomena exist;
they do not recognize the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya), and thus they calculate according to the Vaipulya.
Because the whole does not exist, the parts do not exist.
Because the pillar does not exist, the four atoms do not exist.
Because the person does not exist, the five aggregates do not exist.
If one reckons that all dharmas are non-existent,
this is merely a superficial view that fails to recognize conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Furthermore, both have lost the two truths.
Since Sāṃmitīya does not know that the nature of all phenomena is empty,
he likewise does not recognize that all phenomena exist through the conditions of inversion.
Once the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is lost, the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is likewise lost.
Therefore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
"You refute the meaning of the emptiness of all phenomena through their dependent origination."
This would then destroy all other conventional phenomena;
this is precisely the refutation of the meaning of emptiness,
for it is the refutation of all existent dharmas.
It is further said:
"Because emptiness exists,
all phenomena are established."
If the meaning of emptiness did not exist,
nothing at all would be established; therefore,
the Sautrāntikas do not understand the meaning of emptiness.

Both truths are lost. Next, the Vaipulya [teachings] clarify that all phenomena are empty, thereby losing the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Since the conventional truth is lost, [the ultimate truth is also lost].
One would thus lose the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Therefore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states at its outset:
"Hearing the Mahāyāna teaching of ultimate emptiness..."
One does not know for what causes and conditions things are empty.
If all were empty, then there would be no retribution for sins or merits.
In such a case, one would lose both the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Therefore, the Vaipulya [teachings] do not understand that the two truths possess both existence and non-existence. Why is this so?
Because emptiness is the emptiness of existence.
Since there is already this loss,
it is precisely the loss of emptiness;
furthermore, existence itself is emptiness.
The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Phenomena produced through causes and conditions, I declare to be emptiness.
Since they are emptiness itself, to lose [the understanding of] existence is to lose emptiness.
Since emptiness is thus,
existence is likewise. For this reason:
Both of these individuals have lost the two truths.
Because they have both lost the two truths,
this refutation is intended to cause them to recognize the Tathāgata’s two truths.
Question: Who is it that loses the two truths?
Explanation: To speak in general terms.
There are two kinds of people who lose the two truths:
first, those who do not study the two truths and thus lose them;
second, those who study the two truths and yet lose them.
Generally, all instances of losing the two truths do not exceed these two types.
If it concerns the *Śata-śāstra*,
it refers to the conditions for losing the two truths due to not studying them.
Why is this? The *Śata-śāstra* directly refutes the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*),
who do not understand that the nature of all phenomena is empty.
They do not recognize the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Since they do not know that the nature of all phenomena is empty,
they likewise do not know that all phenomena exist through the conditions of inversion (*viparyāsa*).
Because they do not understand conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), the Bodhisattva Deva,
from the beginning, refuted the existence of the intrinsic nature (dharmatā) of all phenomena.
Ultimately, nothing exists at all.

Next, in the "Chapter on Refuting Emptiness," the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) is refuted. Having thus completed the refutation of the externalists' doctrine of the existence of intrinsic nature and their notion of the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
Thereafter, he demonstrates the two truths based on the causes and conditions of the Tathāgata:
he clarifies that the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya),
and that there is no fault in speaking in accordance with worldly convention (saṃvṛtisatya).
This is precisely the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). By refuting both emptiness and existence, it demonstrates the two truths;
such is the function of the *Śata-śāstra*.
Next, regarding the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*,
it fully refutes two kinds of errors;
whereas the *Śata-śāstra* merely refutes the error of not studying the two truths and the conditions for the two truths.
The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* fully refutes both the failure to learn the two truths and the failure to realize the two truths despite having studied them.
Why is this? Because the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* primarily refutes internal [Buddhist] views while secondarily refuting external [non-Buddhist] ones.
Directly refuting those within [the Buddhist fold],
one correctly refutes their failure to understand the two truths and the conditions for the two truths;
indirectly refuting those without [the Buddhist fold].
This refutes the error of failing to study the two truths and thereby losing the conditions for the two truths;
it refutes the failure to study the two truths and the resulting loss of the two truths,
as in the *Śata-śāstra*.
Regarding those who destroy the study of the two truths and lose the two truths,
there are further two types:
the first are those who correctly refute the Mahāyāna.
Second, it refutes the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) from the side:
those who study the Two Truths in the Mahāyāna lose the Two Truths,
while those in the Lesser Vehicle do not recognize the Two Truths and thus lose the Two Truths.
Those of the Hīnayāna who do not recognize the two truths and have lost the two truths are precisely the aforementioned Pūrṇa and Sāṃmitīya;
both fail to recognize the two truths.
Śāriputra, you perceive that the nature of all phenomena exists;
you do not know that the nature of all phenomena is empty. Since you do not know that their nature is empty, [you do not understand].
That is to say, they do not recognize that all phenomena exist through inversion;
they do not know that their nature is empty;
and they do not recognize the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya).
Not knowing that there is perversion is precisely not recognizing conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
