Next, regarding the failure to recognize the two truths in the Vaipulya [sūtras]:
It is not yet known what school this person belongs to.
If he is a student of the Hīnayāna,
then his drawing of the [mandala] would give rise to false views.
Since the existence of parts is absent, the possessor of parts is likewise non-existent;
yet one gives rise to false views regarding existence.
If such a person is a student of the Mahāyāna, [they will fall into error].
Thus, upon hearing the Mahāyāna teachings, they give rise to wrong views;
hearing the teaching that all things are ultimately empty,
they do not understand for what causes and conditions they are empty.
If all things are ultimately empty,
how can one differentiate between offenses, merit, and their retributions?
If there were such offenses and merits, they could not be empty.
To speculate on emptiness is to give rise to false views.
Once the view of emptiness arises, one fails to recognize conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Since one does not recognize conventional truth...
Thus, one fails to recognize the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Furthermore, because this emptiness is an emptiness of false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi-śūnyatā*), both truths are lost.
Question: The Tripiṭaka clarifies that all phenomena exist.
How, then, can one give rise to wrong views regarding the Tripiṭaka?
Explanation:
Even among the non-Buddhists,
one may still give rise to false views,
as it is said regarding the six teachers: [text follows].
Regarding such views as "there is no black karma and no retribution for black karma," even among non-Buddhists,
one may still give rise to such false views.
How much more so within the Tripiṭaka—could one possibly give rise to false views?
This refers to the Hīnayāna’s failure to recognize the two truths and its loss of the two truths.
Next, regarding the Mahāyāna’s loss of the two truths:
Those who study the Mahāyāna have lost the two truths.
Nāgārjuna appeared in this world specifically for such people,
composing this *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra* (Great Treatise on Great Wisdom).
Both [of these] are failures to study the two truths and failures regarding the two truths.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of failure concerning the two truths in the Mahāyāna.
First, studying the two truths to perfect the two truths of nature;
second, studying the two truths to perfect the one truth.
Regarding the former, the Hīnayāna has two faults.
The first [view] errs regarding the two truths by asserting that they possess a single nature;
the second errs regarding the two truths through a perverted emptiness.
Now, the Mahāyāna likewise incurs both errors.
As in the aforementioned Buddha-dharma, there are four ways of losing the two truths:
losing the two truths through learning the two truths,
and [losing] the two truths of the perfected nature.
To hear that there is abiding in existence is to hear that one dwells in emptiness;
this is as explained in the opening chapter from the beginning.
There is that which exists and can be affirmed;
there is that which does not exist and can be denied; there is that which exists and can be affirmed.
Existence does not arise from non-existence;
thus, existence can become non-existence.
Non-existence does not arise from existence.
Existence does not arise from non-existence;
this existence is self-existent.
Non-existence does not arise from existence.
This non-existence is non-existent by its own nature;
because it exists by its own nature, it is existent;
because it is non-existent by its own nature, it is non-existent.
This refers to the loss of both causes and conditions, and the loss of the two natures becoming one.
It means that because the non-dual becomes dual, there is a loss.
Regarding the statement that those who study the Two Truths lose the Two Truths and establish only One Truth, there are two types.
First, by studying the two truths, one accomplishes the truth of emptiness;
second, by studying the two truths, one accomplishes the truth of existence.
Regarding how one accomplishes the single truth of emptiness by studying the two truths:
The existence of all phenomena through inversion is called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The true knowledge of the emptiness of intrinsic nature by the noble ones (*ārya*) is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
It is clarified that the existence [of phenomena] through inversion is not their true nature, whereas emptiness is what is correct.
Why is this? Because the noble ones truly know that the nature of all phenomena is empty;
therefore, they know.
The emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is precisely this.
Because this person hears of emptiness, they are empty;
hearing of existence is likewise empty.
Studying the two truths results only in the single truth of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
There are two meanings to studying the two truths so as to result in the single truth of existence (*bhava*).
First is the *svalakṣaṇa-dvaya-satya* (the two truths of particular characteristics);
second is the "mind without objects.
Regarding the *svalakṣaṇa-dvaya-satya*:
The sūtra clarifies that form is empty of the nature of form.
Regarding this, it says:
"That which is the emptiness of the nature of form..."
This clarifies that form has no fixed nature, yet it is not the case that form is entirely non-existent.
It is like a rat that has eaten the flesh from within a chestnut; though the flesh is gone, the chestnut still possesses its husk and its shape remains perfectly intact.
Because there is no kernel within the chestnut, one says the chestnut is empty;
it is not because there is no chestnut at all that one says the chestnut is empty.
Thus, emptiness and existence together constitute existence.
Regarding the statement that "the mind has no referent":
this principle has been current for a very long time;
it existed even prior to Master Kumārajīva.
During the time of Dao’an and Zhu Fahu,
this principle already existed; as for what is called the "principle of the mind being non-existent," it is as follows:
It also cites a sutra which says:
"As for form, the nature of form is empty.
This clarifies that form itself cannot be made empty.
It is merely that the mind is empty.
Because one has attained the contemplation of emptiness, one says that form is empty;
yet form itself can never actually become empty.
Master Zhao clarifies that this interpretation is correct in its attainment of spiritual stillness,
but mistaken in its view of the emptiness of phenomena.
To attain a state of divine stillness is to clarify that the mind is empty;
this statement is correct.
Form, however, cannot be made empty.
This interpretation is erroneous.
However, both of these two explanations are instances of learning the Two Truths while failing to realize the Two Truths.
One loses the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and fails to recognize the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
To fail to recognize the ultimate truth is precisely to fail to recognize the conventional truth. Why is this?
This is the existence of emptiness.
To lose existence is to lose emptiness;
furthermore, even if one were to attain a single existence.
Since this existence is an existence that possesses views,
both truths are lost. The same applies to the extreme of emptiness.
Therefore, both [aspects of] the two truths are lost.
To lose the two truths is to lose the conventional;
to lose the conventional is to lose the middle way.
In this, both the provisional principle and the teaching are lost.
To study the two truths as being established by nature is likewise to lose everything.
To hear of two yet not recognize them as non-dual is to lose the Middle;
to lose the Middle is to lose the Provisional.
This is not a fault of mutual dependence;
rather, within this fault, there is the loss of the conventional designation. Why is this so?
Because the provisional is itself the middle.
Those who study the two truths while losing the two truths have lost both simultaneously and thus do not recognize the two truths.
They lose the principle of the two truths;
thus, they all lose the Great [Vehicle]. This consists of three sections:
first, studying the two truths as if they were a single truth.
To lose the two truths is to lose everything.
Second, by studying the two truths, one perfects the two truths of nature.
To lose the two truths is to lose everything.
Third, those who do not recognize the two truths lose both truths;
thus they suffer every possible loss. What kind of person can such individuals be called?
These are merely mad and deluded people.
For the sake of such individuals,
the four reliances transcend the world to refute them.
There are two Bodhisattvas who appear in the world.
When Bodhisattva Deva appears in the world,
he destroys the failure to recognize the Two Truths and the loss of the Two Truths.
The Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna appeared in the world and refuted those who studied the two truths while losing the two truths.
These two bodhisattvas...
This is the perfection of the remedy for destroying illness.
Not only does Śākyamuni Buddha require these two bodhisattvas,
but so too do all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Both of these two bodhisattvas are required. Why is this?
Because these two bodhisattvas encompass all bodhisattvas.
The two errors encompass all errors;
by refuting these two errors,
one establishes the entirety of the teaching.
Why is this? These two faults obstruct the two truths;
one must destroy these two faults.
Thus, the two truths are universal;
when the two truths are universal, all sutras are validated.
Therefore, it is known that this is so.
The Three Treatises are inconceivable;
thus, those in Guanzhong sighed, saying,
"The texts of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and *Śata-śāstra* do not yet equal this."
Furthermore, people lack universal discernment;
who could correct them?
Upon his arrival, he sighed and said:
Only after this may those who discuss the Way begin to engage in discourse on reality.
Such is the nature of ultimate truth.
Why is this? Because these errors do not exceed these two.
Since both the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and the *Śata-śāstra* have already refuted these two errors, [the opponent's position is untenable].
The Two Truths are universally applicable;
because the Two Truths are applied to explain all teachings,
the Three Treatises possess great benefit.
The general meaning is as follows.
Next, regarding those who debate according to the numerical categories (saṃkhyā):
such persons do not understand the two truths (satyadvaya).
They do not understand that the nature of all phenomena is empty;
they merely perceive the nature of all phenomena as existent,
asserting that everything exists.
Not recognizing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*),
and thus not recognizing that the nature of all phenomena is emptiness,
one does not understand that all phenomena exist through causes and conditions.
Because they do not recognize either of the two truths,
they lose the two truths. This refers to the proponents of the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*.
According to the tenets of that treatise, it is identical to the Tripiṭaka.
Why? Because its introduction states:
"Therefore, I wish to correctly discuss the true meaning within the Tripiṭaka."
Thus, they are the same as the Sautrāntikas in failing to recognize the two truths.
If, according to their own tenets, the meaning of the two truths were present,
they would have clarified the twofold emptiness of persons and phenomena.
However, while śrāvakas understand emptiness,
they ultimately do not realize the emptiness of intrinsic nature. Why is this?
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"In the Dharma for śrāvakas, the Buddha did not teach the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) or the emptiness of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*)."
Because they do not explain that intrinsic nature is empty,
they do not recognize the ultimate truth; because they do not recognize the ultimate truth, [they do not realize it].
This means they do not understand conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
If that were so, both [the Sarvāstivādins and the Sāṃkhyas] would fail to grasp the two truths;
for such people as these all lose sight of the two truths.
For this reason, the Buddhas have taught the two truths,
and the Bodhisattvas have set forth the doctrine of the two truths,
so as to cause sentient beings to recognize the two truths.
To understand the two truths is to understand all provisional designations (*prajñapti*) and so forth within them.
For this reason, it is said that the two truths possess great benefit.
Previously, it was explained that there are two kinds of loss regarding the two truths.
First, the failure to recognize the two truths. Regarding those who fail to recognize the two truths, there are two types in the world: the Sāṃkhyas and the Vaiśeṣikas.
The Sāṃkhyas do not understand that the nature of all phenomena is emptiness.
He merely clarifies that the nature of all phenomena exists;
this person does not recognize the emptiness of nature and thus lacks the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
The proponent argues that although one may clearly understand the emptiness of all phenomena,
this is the emptiness of the Śrāvaka-dharma and not the ultimate emptiness (paramārtha-śūnyatā) of the present context.
Because the intrinsic emptiness of all phenomena is now taken as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*),
the treatise states:
"The true knowledge of the nature of emptiness by the noble ones (*ārya*) is called the ultimate."
The *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* does not contain this emptiness.
How is this known? Because the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* correctly elucidates the teachings of the Tripiṭaka.
Nāgārjuna’s judgment states:
Within the teachings for the śrāvakas,
the Buddha did not teach that all phenomena are empty of their own characteristics (svalakṣaṇa-śūnya) or empty of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-śūnya).
Since they are empty because they lack intrinsic nature,
those [dharmas] do not exist as ultimate truth;
for within them, there is no absence of the two emptinesses of person and phenomena.
He cites the *Rādha-gītā-sūtra* to clarify the emptiness of both persons and phenomena; however,
this [text] merely uses the analysis of phenomena to clarify the emptiness of phenomena.
This does not clarify the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).
This [critique] is based on a single section of the *Abhidharma*;
the *Abhidharma* does not clarify emptiness.
The *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* elucidates emptiness.
If this is the case, then in relation to the *Abhidharma-piṭaka*, there are two truths;
however, in relation to the Mahāyāna, there are no two truths.
However, this is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya). Why?
Because now [we speak of] the Mahāyāna.
It is precisely because the intrinsic emptiness of all phenomena constitutes the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
They merely deconstruct phenomena to clarify emptiness;
therefore, they lack the ultimate truth.
Question: For what purpose is this statement used?
Explanation: It is intended to explain a single phrase within the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*.
That treatise states:
"You now hear what is called conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and claim it to be ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
We shall now employ the explanations of the Sāṃkhya and other schools to analyze this statement."
Question: If one hears of the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and takes it to be the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), how is this to be understood? Answer:
The Abhidharma also elucidates the meaning of the two truths.
That is to say, the sixteen truths of reality— such as suffering, impermanence, and so forth— are the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya),
while the suffering of physical affliction by weapons, staves, and the like is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
This is how he distinguishes the two truths based on both phenomena and principle.
Now, it is clear that this judgment regarding the two truths is erroneous. Why is this so?
Principle and phenomena are both conventional truths;
the emptiness of the nature of all dharmas is the ultimate truth.
Impermanence and so forth belong to the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya),
whereas [the realization that] they are [empty] is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya); therefore, it is said:
Hearing the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), they claim it is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya);
for this reason, they fall into error. Since the two truths have thus been inverted, [the system is undermined].
Then everything would be inverted.
Why? Because all Buddhas teach the Dharma by relying upon the two truths.
Since the two truths are inverted,
everything is inverted;
thus, one falls into a state of error.
Next, regarding the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*’s claim that what is heard as conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*):
this clarifies that all phenomena are conventionally existent, while the emptiness resulting from the deconstruction of phenomena constitutes the ultimate truth.
Now it is clarified:
that all dharmas possess the emptiness of disintegration is entirely a matter of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Why is this? Now, the two truths are distinguished based on the emptiness of intrinsic nature and the non-emptiness of intrinsic nature;
the emptiness of intrinsic nature constitutes the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).

It is not that emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) constitutes conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Since you dismantle the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) rather than the emptiness of intrinsic nature, this [emptiness of phenomena] is conventional truth.
You claim that because it pertains to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), you have fallen into error.
Why? Because your own thesis states that you are correctly elucidating the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*).
Nāgārjuna said:
Because the Buddha did not teach the emptiness of intrinsic nature within the Tripitaka,
there is no ultimate truth (paramārtha).
If there were an ultimate truth (paramārtha), it would contradict the tenets of your own treatise;
therefore, one should simply say: "For this reason, I wish to correctly discourse upon the true meaning of the Mahāyāna."
Furthermore, the *Tattvaviniścaya-śāstra* transmits the meaning of the Tripitaka as being the emptiness of intrinsic nature;
because it is the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
There is no ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya);
one is defeated whether advancing or retreating.
This is not a superficial refutation.
The principle is thus. Next,
to clarify those who study the two truths yet lose the two truths,
the Great Master said:
This is like losing a lapis lazuli gem.
For example, it is as if one were bathing in a great pond and lost a lapis lazuli gem;
though all the people search for the gem, they do not find it.
Each person joyfully took out a piece of *tiwashi* stone,
only to realize it was not genuine;
in truth, they had mistaken fish eyes for "night-shining" gems.
This is precisely the case of one who studies the two truths yet fails to recognize the two truths.
Question: Does such a person, upon hearing this conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), consider it to be the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya)?
Explanation: [As follows].
It can also be obtained.
This has two meanings.
The first is to clarify it by means of refutation.
Second, regarding the clarification through establishment and refutation:
within the treatise, one cross-examines and refutes the myriad dharmas.
The five phrases of the "Vertical Washing" state:
"All things are ultimately non-existent;
that is what he calls the ultimate truth (paramārtha)."
This is because it is negated by ultimate truth, and thus all things are empty.
Those who provide unskillful expositions of the Three Treatises also maintain this view.
It is said that these refutations and washings constitute the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Now it is clarified:
these are actually conventional truths (*saṃvṛti-satya*) which are [erroneously] called the ultimate truth.
How is this known? Take, for example, the sixteen modes of knowledge regarding the emptiness of self:
within these sixteen modes of knowledge, there is no self.
"Is this the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) or the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya)?
He replied: 'The sixteen types of knowledge-and-vision [demonstrate] that the self is empty.'"
This is the emptiness of conventional truth.
Why? Because, in reality, there is no self characterized by the sixteen types of views and cognitions.
The non-Buddhists hold inverted views, asserting that there is a self;
this refutes the sixteen types of speculative views regarding the self.
As for the emptiness of the self in these sixteen views:
This is the emptiness of conventional truth.
Now it is likewise:
in reality, these various phenomena do not exist.
This refers specifically to the inversion of perceiving existence.
Now, by refuting this arbitrary assertion, it is clarified that all phenomena are empty;
thus, this is the emptiness of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Nor is it the conventional truth;
rather, it is that which is free from the conventional truth.
It is free from all such phenomena.
This is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya). For this reason,
all phenomena (dharmas) are deconstructed.
That there is nothing whatsoever is conventional truth;
it is because they do not understand this.
This refers to what is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya). Therefore, they fall into error;
thus, they hear of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and mistake it for the ultimate truth.
Regarding the statement of the thesis:
it concerns the non-obstruction of causes and conditions within the two truths,
as explained in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*.
"Those phenomena produced through causes and conditions—
I say they are emptiness;
they are provisional designations."
This is precisely the Middle Way.
It is unimpeded both horizontally and vertically.
When the provisional is identical to the middle, it is vertically unimpeded.
The two do not obstruct non-duality;
non-duality does not obstruct the two.
The two function as the utility of non-duality.
Non-duality functions as duality.
"The dharmas produced by causes and conditions, I say, are themselves emptiness"—
this is horizontal non-obstruction.
Existence does not obstruct emptiness;
emptiness does not obstruct existence.
Existence functions as the utility of emptiness.
Emptiness is functional.
How could it be that emptiness alone is unimpeded?
Rather, it is within the midst of existence that all dharmas are unimpeded.
As explained in the *Avataṃsaka*,
the buddha-fields of the three periods of time are unimpeded— whether pure or defiled, long or short— and these fields are mutually unimpeded.
Such non-obstruction is called the Noble Truth (*āryasatya*).
When a bodhisattva attains non-obstruction,
it is not that all phenomena are obstructed; rather,
the bodhisattva attains the contemplation of non-obstruction.
It causes all dharmas to be unimpeded.
By attaining unimpeded supernormal powers, one renders all dharmas unimpeded;
this is truly because all dharmas are themselves unimpeded.
Because the Bodhisattva’s essence is unimpeded with respect to phenomena,
the Bodhisattva attains unimpeded contemplation. Because they attain unimpeded contemplation, [they realize this].
They attain unimpeded eloquence and unimpeded supernormal powers.
If all phenomena were obstructed, [these would not be possible].
If a bodhisattva attains unimpeded supernormal powers and causes others to become unimpeded,
that bodhisattva incurs a transgression.
Because all phenomena are inherently unimpeded,
the bodhisattva attains unimpeded contemplation and unimpeded supernormal powers.
One attains unimpeded eloquence.
Because it is thus unimpeded,
it is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
If one follows the approach of the former masters, the two truths are thus defined:
the three provisional designations constitute the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), while the fourfold forgetting constitutes the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
The three provisional designations cannot constitute the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
The fourfold forgetting cannot constitute the conventional truth (saṃvṛti).
The ultimate truth cannot possess names or characteristics (nāma-lakṣaṇa).
In the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), names and characteristics cannot be non-existent.
Therefore, the Great Master said:
"That [text] provides two interpretations for the meaning of 'orange'."
Upon hearing it said that all phenomena are empty,
he immediately placed [the object] within a seat of ultimate truth;
upon hearing it said that all phenomena exist...
It is then placed within the ladder of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya):
in conventional truth, emptiness is not attained;
in ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), existence is not attained.
Thus, both existence and non-existence are obstructive;
because they are obstructive, they are all merely conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). He then said:
I possess both the ultimate and conventional truths.
How could they both be merely conventional truth?
The explanation says:
That which is unimpeded is entirely conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Since you yourself regard it as ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya),
you have merely heard that conventional truth is ultimate truth.
Those who hold such views as these have both lost the Tathāgata’s two truths and are unable to understand the profound meaning of the Buddha-dharma.
If one can know the two truths,
then one knows the profound meaning of the Buddha-dharma. Why is this?
To recognize that the two truths of the Abhidharma are the two truths of the Abhidharma,
and to know that these two truths are both merely conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya),
and thus never to study these two truths [as ultimate], is [the correct approach].
The two truths of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Consciousness-Only Treatise) are the two truths of analytical dharma (*prabheda-dharma*) as established in the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi);
they are not the two truths of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) of all dharmas.
Because consciousness has existed from the beginning, those who attain the Mahāyāna perceive these as the two truths of obstructed existence.
They recognize the two truths without obstruction regarding all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Because they recognize these two truths in this way,
they understand the profound meaning of the Buddha-dharma.
The verse says:
"If a person cannot discern the two truths,
they will not know the true meaning of the profound Buddha-dharma."
If it were the reverse,
one should say: "If a person can thoroughly understand and discern the two truths,
then they will know the true meaning within the profound Buddha-dharma."
For this reason,
it is said that the two truths possess great benefit. Thus far,
according to the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, the gains and losses regarding the two truths have been clarified in this manner.
Next, we shall examine the two truths of gain and loss based on the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*.
The treatise states:
"If a person knows the two truths..."
Thus, one attains self-benefit, benefit for others, and mutual benefit;
if one does not know the two truths,
one will not attain these three benefits.
These two treatises mutually clarify their respective strengths and weaknesses.

As for what is called benefiting oneself, benefiting others, and benefiting both, it refers to the thorough understanding of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
The arising of the wisdom of reality through skillful means is called self-benefit;
the thorough understanding of ultimate truth and conventional truth,
resulting in the arising of the wisdom of reality through skillful means, is called benefit for others.
To fully comprehend both the ultimate and conventional truths and to give rise to the two types of wisdom is called "common benefit.
Second, the bodhisattva personally realizes both the ultimate and conventional truths.
The arising of the two wisdoms of means and reality is called self-benefit.
The Bodhisattva has awakened to them as they truly are,
and now he likewise explains them as they truly are.
Causing sentient beings to likewise comprehend the two truths— the ultimate and the conventional— and thereby generate the two wisdoms— the provisional and the real— is called benefiting others.
When both oneself and others comprehend the two truths and both generate the two wisdoms, it is called mutual benefit.
Question: What is the difference between these two types of twofold wisdom?
Explanation: The former distinguishes the two wisdoms based on the ultimate (paramārtha) and the conventional (saṃvṛti).
Regarding the subsequent classification of the two wisdoms based on self and other, internal and external:

as for the prior classification of the two wisdoms based on the ultimate and conventional truths, it consists of the realization of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

The knowledge of means that realizes ultimate truth and conventional truth is called "actual skillful means wisdom. The knowledge of actual reality that realizes ultimate truth and conventional truth is called "actual skillful means wisdom."
This concludes the discernment of the two truths and the two wisdoms.
Subsequently, regarding the distinction between self and other, or internal and external:
internally awakening to the two truths is termed "real wisdom" (bhūta-jñāna).
To explain the two truths to others is called the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*).
This involves opening up the two truths within the context of ultimate wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*),
and opening up the two truths within the context of the wisdom of skillful means.
This is precisely the discernment of the two wisdoms based on internal self-awakening and external transformation of others.
Regarding those who obtain the benefits of these two wisdoms,
it is because these two wisdoms are clearly the parents of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* says:
"Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of Bodhisattvas; Upāya is their father.
They are the guides of all beings."
Because there is nothing that does not arise from this,
these two types of wisdom are the parents of all Buddhas. If one thoroughly understands the two truths, [one attains enlightenment].
Thus, there are two kinds of wisdom.
Because there are these two kinds of wisdom,
there are the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
If one does not comprehend the two truths,
then there is no non-dual wisdom;
if there is no non-dual wisdom, then there are no Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Thus, one should know that the teaching of the two truths brings great benefit.
Furthermore, as for this benefit:
He fully understands the conventional truth and the ultimate truth,
thereby transcending the stage of ordinary beings;
he fully understands the ultimate truth and the conventional truth.
Distant from the stage of the two vehicles;
distant from the stage of ordinary beings;
distant from the stage of the two vehicles.
This is the stage of the bodhisattva;
if one does not understand the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) and the conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya),
one will not transcend the stages of the two vehicles.
They do not comprehend the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya);
they do not leave the stage of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana-bhūmi), nor do they leave these two stages.
That is, within the perilous path of five hundred yojanas;
if one realizes the two truths,
one immediately emerges beyond those five hundred yojanas.
Entering the stage of a bodhisattva,
one is born into the family of the Buddhas,
possessing a noble and exalted lineage.
For this reason, thoroughly understanding the two truths brings great benefit.
Furthermore, as for that benefit:
it is the departure from the two views of annihilationism and eternalism.
One thoroughly understands the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya),
thereby departing from the view of eternalism;
one thoroughly understands the ultimate truth and the conventional truth, thereby departing from the view of nihilism.
Free from the two views of annihilationism and eternalism,
one practices the noble Middle Way and perceives the Buddha-nature.
If one does not comprehend the two truths,
one will not practice the Middle Way and will not perceive the Buddha-nature.
If one does not see the Buddha-nature,
there is no Buddha who possesses such a nature.
If one thoroughly understands the two truths, [one realizes this].
Thus, one departs from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, practices the Middle Way,
and perceives the Buddha-nature.
This refers to those such as the Buddha of Existence (Svabhāva-buddha). For this reason,
one should know that the two truths of consciousness provide great benefit.
The brief explanation of gain, loss, and benefit is thus.
Next is the explanation of the meaning of awakening to the teaching and generating wisdom;
this meaning is difficult to understand.
If it is for the sake of generating wisdom?
The Master’s traditional teaching says:
"One attains awakening by receiving the instruction."
Two kinds of wisdom arise;
when the teaching is transformed, it is termed the "object.
If one does not awaken to this, wisdom will not arise.
Regarding those who do not awaken:
having heard that there is activity and understanding,
they immediately abide in activity.
There is neither manifestation nor existence;
hearing that there is no action and no liberation,
one abides in non-existence.
That there is nothing that does not manifest and nothing that is not non-existent is called "non-awakening.
As for what is called "awakening":
Hearing of existence, one does not abide in existence;
existence indicates non-existence.
Hearing of non-existence, one does not abide in non-existence.
It is not that non-manifestation (avijñapti) does not exist;
it is designated as "awakening" (bodhi).
How could an action be awakening?
Is it that one awakens to the non-duality of neither existence nor non-existence?
Or is it that one awakens to the duality of existence and non-existence? If it were by means of the duality of existence and non-existence—
Realizing that which is neither existent nor non-existent is non-duality;
one should give rise to the wisdom of non-duality.
How could one give rise to dualistic wisdom?
If one says that awakening consists in [discerning] the two— existence and non-existence—
this is merely awakening to the teaching and should not be considered awakening to the principle. Since one does not awaken to the principle, [it is not true awakening].
How can that be called awakening?
It is difficult to clarify whether one has advanced or retreated; thus, it remains unexplained, and so forth.
Next, the clarification that the two truths are the meaning of the teaching:
since the time of Xinghuang of Sheshan,
all have clarified that the two truths are the teaching.
Therefore, Master Shishou’s own commentary on the *Two Truths* (*Er-di-shu*) states:
"The Two Truths are the wondrous teaching that expresses the Middle Way;
they are the ultimate exposition of the limits of literary expression."
The Way is neither existence nor non-existence;
it is through the mediation of existence and non-existence that the Way is revealed.
Principle is neither one nor two.
By means of the one and the two, the principle is clarified;
therefore, we know that the two truths are the teaching.
There are two reasons for clarifying that the Two Truths constitute the teaching:
first, to address others;
second, to explain the sūtras and śāstras.
In order to clarify for others that the two truths are the objective domain,
there are four kinds of Dharma-jewels therein; these are called the Jewel of the Teaching (deśanā-dharmaratna).
The Dharma-jewel of the objective realm;
the Dharma-jewel of unconditioned fruition;
the Dharma-jewel of virtuous karma.
The two truths are the Jewel of the Dharma as the objective realm.
Whether a Buddha appears or not, this realm always exists.
To be deluded regarding it results in the chaotic proliferation of the six realms of existence.
Because upon awakening to it, there are the three vehicles and ten stages;
thus, the two truths are the objects of delusion and awakening.
Now, in contrast to that, it is clarified that the two truths are the teaching.
Regarding the explanation of the sūtras and śāstras,
the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
"The Buddhas, relying upon the two truths, teach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings."
The *Śata-śāstra* is likewise.
All Buddhas always rely upon the two truths;
both of these are real and not false speech.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"The bodhisattva dwells within the two truths and preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings."
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"The conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is itself the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
It is only in accordance with sentient beings that two truths are spoken of."
Because the sutras clarify that the two truths are the teaching;
now, our school clarifies that the two truths are the teaching.
This is to have mastered the Master’s words.
Furthermore, one knows their ultimate intention.
Why? Because one knows it is intended for the sake of others.
I understand this to be an exegesis of the sūtras and śāstras;
however, this meaning remains difficult to resolve. Why is that?
You say that the two truths are the teaching; yet,
while it is said that there are two truths within the two truths,
it has not been stated that there are no two truths apart from the two truths.
If the two truths already exist,
then one is the same as other schools; if one is not the same as other schools, [then the two truths do not exist].
If the two truths exist only when the two truths are taught,
then before the two truths have been taught, there should be no two truths. Furthermore, this is difficult to maintain.
When the two truths are taught, for the first time there are the two truths;
before the two truths were taught, the two truths did not exist.
When the emptiness of form is taught, for the first time there is the emptiness of form.
If it were not taught that form is empty, there would be no emptiness of form;
yet even before it was taught,
the emptiness of form already existed.
If that were so, even before the two truths have been explained,
the two truths would already exist;
and their existing [prior to being explained] is the same as what others say, and so forth.
However, the two truths are the meaning of the teaching;
if one can comprehend the meaning of the two truths,
then the three treatises may also be understood.
If one does not understand this meaning,
the meaning of the two truths cannot be understood,
and the treatise in three sections likewise cannot be understood.
Why is this? You clarify that the two truths are the objects of cognition;
you now clarify that the two truths are the teaching.
The teaching of the Dharma is the instruction.
Are the two truths also the instruction?
If the two truths are the instruction...
This would contradict the treatise.
The treatise states:
"The Buddhas teach the Dharma by relying on the two truths."
If it is suddenly asked whether the two truths are the teaching,
the explanation is as follows:
there are two kinds of two truths.
First, the truth of reality (*tattva-satya*); second, the truth of teaching (*deśanā-satya*).
Regarding the truth of reality, as stated in the treatise:
"The nature of all phenomena is emptiness."
What the world mistakenly regards as existing is considered real by worldly people; therefore,
it is called a truth (satya).
The noble ones and sages truly know inversion;
for them, the emptiness of intrinsic nature is reality,
and thus it is called a truth (satya).
This refers to the two truths regarding the [Four] Truths.
The Buddhas rely upon these to teach;
they are called the "truths of the teaching" (*deśanā-satya*).
Question: Why is the teaching called "truth" (*satya*)?
Answer: There are several meanings.
First, because it is taught in accordance with reality.
What is spoken is also real;
therefore, it is called "truth" (*satya*).
Second, it is the Tathāgata’s word of sincere truth.
For this reason, it is called a truth (*satya*).
Third, it is said that there exists non-informative action (*avijñapti*),
which is truly capable of manifesting the Path.
For this reason, it is called "truth" (satya).
Why are the teachings of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) not called truth?
What is taught by the non-Buddhists cannot manifest the Path; therefore,
it cannot be called a Truth (satya).
That which is taught by all Buddhas truly expresses the Path; therefore,
it is called "Truth" (*satya*).
Fourth, the teaching of the Dharma truly benefits those with whom it is shared;
for this reason, it is called "Truth.
As for the teachings of the non-Buddhists:
If they cannot truly benefit conditions,
they cannot be called truths (satya).
This applies to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
It is truly able to benefit conditions;
therefore, it is called a truth (*satya*).
Fifth, its teaching is non-erroneous.
For this reason, it is called "truth" (*satya*).
This is as explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* regarding the meaning of the single ultimate truth (*eka-satya*) spoken by the Tathāgata.
That which is free from inversion is called the single ultimate truth;
the present case is likewise so.
Because that which is taught is non-erroneous,
it is called "truth" (*satya*). As for what is taught by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), [it is not so].
All these are inverted and cannot be called truths;
so it is taught by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
It is free from inversion;
therefore, it is called "truth" (*satya*).
Sixth, one attains realization in accordance with reality.
Because it is spoken according to reality, it is called "truth" (*satya*).
Thus, a sutra says: "One who speaks as it is, one who speaks the truth, one whose speech is not otherwise, one whose speech is not deceptive."
This is because the Tathāgata is truthful and not false;
thus, "teaching" (jiao) is termed "truth" (di).
Next, the truths are explained.
By what causes and conditions is it called "truth" (*satya*)? Is it named after subjective cognition,
or is it designated according to its objective referent?
Is it from the perspective of understanding (*jñāna*) or from the perspective of the faculty (*indriya*)?
The explanation says:
regarding the Truths, it is named from the perspective of the dual aspects of emotional understanding.
However, this meaning has two aspects.
First, the determination of gain and loss regarding the two truths;
second, that which is real for ordinary beings.
That which is called the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is empty of the reality of the noble ones;
that which is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is [the opposite].
This existence refers to existence as it appears in the conventional mind;
this emptiness is the true understanding of emptiness.
To say that conventional existence is a loss is a mistake.
"Truly understanding emptiness constitutes attainment.
This refers to the judgment of the two truths based on the reality of one's mental state. How is this known?
Therefore, the Treatise says:
"The nature of all phenomena is empty;
yet the world, through its inversions, speaks of 'existence,' which is called conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya)."
O worthy noble ones,
the true knowledge of the emptiness of intrinsic nature is called the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Since it is said that this is the true knowledge of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, it is the authentic understanding.
It was stated previously that "perversion" refers to existence; this is what is meant by "sentiment.
If this is so, then one knows that this very sentiment constitutes the true understanding of gain and loss.
This is to distinguish the two truths.
Regarding the phrase "distinguishing the two truths" in the context of the two [aspects]:
it is like form, which has never been either empty or existent.
Ordinary people say that form exists;
for them, what is real is called "truth.
The Noble Ones say that form is empty.
To the noble ones, these are truly called "truths" (satya).
Whether they exist or not,
both are merely matters of conventional sentiment.
Both are errors; for the ordinary person asserts existence,
while the noble one asserts emptiness.
This emptiness and existence must both be washed away and destroyed;
there is no such thing as existence.
There is no such emptiness;
only through ultimate purification does one first come to understand that causes and conditions are empty yet existent.
The emptiness and existence of causes and conditions are themselves neither empty nor existent.
Once one recognizes that they are neither empty nor existent, [one realizes this].
This means that realizing emptiness is itself neither empty nor existent;
the preceding notions of emptiness and existence are both the afflictions to be remedied.
Therefore, both [positions] are erroneous.
By such a principle, it is called the "truth of the teaching" (jiao-di);
by such a principle, it is called the "truth of reality" (yu-di).
"Is this the Teacher’s word?
"Indeed, this is truly the Teacher’s word.
Next, a doubt and objection are raised therein.
Why is this? One preaches the Dharma based on the truths.
Are the truths not the objective sphere (ālambana)?
If it were not an object of cognition, it would contradict the treatise.
The treatise states:
"The noble ones truly know that the nature of all phenomena is empty."
True knowledge is precisely wisdom.
Wisdom must have an object.
The emptiness of intrinsic nature is that very object.
True knowledge is itself wisdom.
If that is so, the two truths are the objects; thus, one relies upon the objects of the two truths.
He preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
When one gives rise to the *Pratītyasamutpādādivibhaṅganirdeśa*, it immediately establishes the meaning of others. Others also say:
The two truths are the object;
the teaching that expounds the names of the two truths is the doctrine.
Therefore, there is the Jewel of the Doctrine as the teaching and the Jewel of the Dharma as the objective realm.
The Four Truths and the Two Truths are the Dharma-jewel as an object;
they are taught as the Four Truths and the Two Truths.
This refers precisely to the Dharma Jewel of the verbal teachings;
it is the same now as well—
how does this differ from others?
If one were to say, "I do not hold this view," it would contradict the treatise.
The treatise states:
The Buddhas rely upon the two truths to preach the Dharma for sentient beings; how, then,
can it be said that the two truths are themselves the teaching?
To proceed or retreat is both untenable.
To support the treatise is to be the same as others;
to differ from others is to contradict the treatise.
Furthermore, another response to the objection is that there are both ultimate truths (*paramārtha-satya*) and conventional truths (*saṃvṛti-satya*); within ultimate truths,
there are both the true ultimate and the conventional ultimate.
Are there ultimate and conventional truths regarding the teachings?

If one says that the teachings also possess ultimate and conventional truths, then according to the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, when one dies, it is unclear how one would die according to that treatise. As for those who die according to the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*: [text continues].
Now, let me ask you this:
when you speak of the conventional, do you say it is conventional?
And when you speak of the ultimate, do you say it is ultimate?
If you claim that this statement is true,
it contradicts your own tenet. Why is this?
According to your position, the truth of teaching (*deśanā-satya*) is merely conventional because it consists of speech;
therefore, one cannot say that the truth of teaching encompasses both the ultimate and the conventional.
If you fear having to revise your statement regarding speech, [then consider this].
If it is said that these are not real,
how can one speak of the teaching of the two truths— the ultimate and the conventional?
If this is the interpretation of the Satyasiddhi-śāstra school, [then...]
It is said: The two truths, ultimate and conventional, are the objects;
these objects consist of the ultimate and the conventional.
To speak of the ultimate and to speak of the conventional—
both of these modes of speaking belong to the conventional truth;
the ultimate is ineffable.
This is spoken in reliance upon conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Now, I ask the masters of the Three Treatises (*Sanlun*):
according to their school, the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the conventional are objects (*viṣaya*).
Within the objective realm, there is the ultimate and the conventional.
You have now clarified that the two truths are a gateway of teaching;
does the truth of the teaching itself also possess the ultimate and the conventional?
Those who do not understand the meaning will certainly say that the teaching on the truths also includes both the ultimate and the conventional. Why?
Because there are two truths.
There are the truth of existence and the truth of teaching.
Within the truth of existence, there are the ultimate and the conventional; within the truth of teaching, there are likewise the ultimate and the conventional.
Question: If one asks whether there are ultimate and conventional truths within the truth of teaching (*deśanā-satya*), the explanation is as follows:
that which is called "conventional" is termed the conventional truth of teaching.
To speak of the ultimate is called the "Ultimate Teaching" (paramārtha-śāsana).
Question: To speak of the conventional is called the "Conventional Teaching";
thus, the teaching is conventional.
Is it true that the teaching expounded is itself the truth?
This "teaching of the truth" is what constitutes verbal instruction.
If that sudden [realization] were the truth,
then the discourse that speaks of the conventional would be the conventional truth;
yet even the discourse that speaks of the truth would likewise be the conventional truth.
This immediately establishes the opponent's position;
the opponent also clarifies that the ultimate truth is truly ineffable.
To rely on conventional discourse to explain the ultimate,
the very discourse explaining the ultimate still belongs to the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
The present case is likewise;
thus, it accords with the traditional interpretation of the Three Treatises.
This is indeed my own position.
Therefore, Cheng-lun Xuanzheng read the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*.
The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* says:
Discourse is conventional truth;
the ultimate truth is ineffable.
If that is so, then all discourse is conventional truth.
How can it be said that both truths are equally the teaching?
Furthermore, if both truths were the teaching, and the teaching were exclusively conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), [then what of ultimate truth?]
Thus, by studying the two truths, one becomes established in a single conventional truth.
Those who have come before have already failed in their attempt to study the two truths and become established in a single truth.
Now you attempt to merge the two truths into one truth;
this is a grave error. Furthermore, it is difficult to maintain.
In your system, the two truths are explained as being the objects [of cognition], wherein both the ultimate and the conventional exist within the object.
In your system, the two truths are explained as being the teachings;
however, the teaching itself is merely the conventional.

This is to ensure the possession of both the ultimate and the conventional truths; for if one were to rely on the conventional alone, one would lose the ultimate truth and become identical to other schools.
If one were to maintain both truths, it would contradict the treatise;
furthermore, the meaning would be untenable.
The treatise states:
Discourse is conventional truth;
the ultimate is ineffable. Furthermore, this is difficult to explain.
If verbal expression were the ultimate truth,
would one now take up the emptiness of verbal expression as the ultimate truth,
or would one take up the empty verbal expression itself as the ultimate truth?
If one takes verbal expression to be true,
then since verbal expression exists,
that would be the ultimate truth.
If you say that the emptiness of verbal expression is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*),
then what is this "emptiness of verbal expression"?
You should simply state that the emptiness of verbal expression is conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) and that the emptiness [of phenomena] is the ultimate truth.
If it is said that only emptiness is the ultimate truth,
is the teaching of emptiness itself true?
If the teaching of emptiness were true, then [the objection] would apply equally to both.
If it is said that both "emptiness is emptiness" and "emptiness is spoken of" are both true principles (satya),
then both "form is emptiness" and "emptiness is form" would also be true principles. [The opponent] objects with the following counter-questions, and so forth.
Having come here, there are four difficulties that remain unresolved;
these shall be explained later.
Now, let us further examine the meaning of gain and loss.
There are generally four types of gain and loss mentioned previously;
here, we shall examine the last one: the failure to learn the two truths regarding the two truths.
If this were merely for the sake of the Hīnayāna,
it would not be worth distinguishing; rather,
it is specifically intended for those who study the two truths yet have lost the true meaning of the two truths.
The *Mingtaji* (Discrimination of Other Schools) analyzes the meaning of the two truths;
the present work also analyzes the meaning of the two truths.
What is the difference between them?
There are ten distinct points for explaining this.
First, it clarifies the meaning of principle and teaching;
others [assert] that the two truths are devoid of principle and teaching.
Regarding the current clarification that while there are both principle and scripture for the two truths, there is neither principle nor scripture for the other:
that [other] clarifies that the two truths are indeed principle.
The three provisional designations are the principle of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);
the four negations are the principle of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Now it is clarified that while the two truths are the teaching, their non-duality is the principle.
The Sūtra says:
"Mañjuśrī, the Dharma is always thus;
for the Dharma King, there is but this one Dharma."
All those who are fearless transcend birth and death by means of a single path.
It is also said:
Regarding all phenomena that exist or do not exist,
one thoroughly realizes them to be neither existent nor non-existent;
thus it is known.
Existence and non-existence are the two aspects of the teaching;
neither existence nor non-existence, nor duality, is the principle.
Thus, both the principle and the teaching are fully present.
If there were only the other [the conventional] and it lacked the two [aspects],
then there would be only the teaching and no underlying principle;
one could say that such worldly phenomena possess words but lack meaning.
At first glance it is thus;
upon further examination, there is nothing to be seized or appropriated.
Why? Because words fundamentally serve to explain meanings.
Since there is no meaning,
what could the syllables possibly signify?
Thus, both reason and scripture are lost.
Now it is clear that existence and non-existence are the teachings;
they express the principle of neither being nor non-being.
This, then, possesses both principle and teaching;
it is the perfection of both principle and teaching.
It is with such an intention that this was said.
This was stated in order to explain the sūtras for the sake of others, and so forth.
Next, it clarifies that the teaching of the two truths gives rise to the two wisdoms, and thus the teaching is renamed as the "object.
Why was this statement made?
It is also to counter the "Coming from" (youlai) view.
The "Coming from" view states:
"The ultimate and the conventional are naturally occurring realms."
The three provisional designations are the realm of the conventional;
the fourfold forgetting is the realm of ultimate truth.
To be deluded regarding them is for the six realms of existence to fall into chaos.
Upon awakening to this, there are the worthies and sages of the Three Vehicles who constantly abide in this state;
thus, if this wisdom arises from cultivation, [it is not inherently existent].
The object is eternally existent,
whereas cognition arises only at the beginning.
Before cognition exists, the object has already been present.
The meaning of the object and wisdom being non-conditional:
now, in contrast to this, it is clarified that the ultimate and the conventional are teachings;
by awakening to these teachings, wisdom arises.
The teaching is transformed and termed "object.
It is an object by virtue of wisdom,
and wisdom by virtue of the object.
The object can act as the domain for cognition;
cognition can act as the domain for the object;
and the object can act as the domain for the capacity of cognition.
The capacity of that which is the object of wisdom and the wisdom itself are non-dual yet dual through their causal conditions.
Question: Where there is duality, there is neither the Path nor the fruit.
For what reason are two [types of] clarity explained?
The explanation says:
it is in order to contrast them with the lack of wisdom regarding objects.
Now it is clear:
by virtue of cognition there is the object,
and by virtue of the object there is cognition.
The non-duality of the two— object and wisdom, cause and condition—
is established. Now, it is clarified that the Two Truths are a gateway of teaching.
This is precisely for the purpose of uprooting the views regarding these two principles.
Those views concerning the two principles are deeply buried;
as long as these two principles exist, they can ultimately never be changed.
For this reason, it is now clarified that there is only one principle and no second principle. Why is this?
When the Tathāgata speaks of existence or non-existence,
it is to manifest the single path;
this very existence and non-existence constitute the gateway to the Way.
This is not the principle.
For this reason, it is clarified that the two truths are the teaching, not the principle itself.
Second is the meaning of having marks and being without marks.
It has been said from of old that the mountain schools (Buddhist monasteries) have attained the meaning of being without marks.
Other schools clearly teach that there are marks;
for what reason do they hold that there are marks?
Why does our mountain gate teach that there are no marks?
The commentary states:
"Existence has the characteristic of existence; non-existence has the characteristic of non-existence."
If existence were without the characteristic of existence, then there would be no existence; if non-existence were without the characteristic of non-existence, [the same would follow].
If there were neither existence nor non-existence,
then the two truths would not exist;
yet, as a matter of principle, the two truths do indeed exist.
That which exists has the characteristic of existence; that which does not exist has the characteristic of non-existence.
This is called the meaning of the characteristic of existence.
Now it is clear:

where there is existence, there is the characteristic of existence, and while there is manifestation, there is no non-existence; where there is non-existence, there is the characteristic of non-existence, and while there is no manifestation, there is no non-non-existence.
Because it neither exists nor does not exist as a non-informative [phenomenon],
it is called the meaning of "signlessness" (animitta). Because it is signless, [it is so named].
Therefore, it is called the gate of teaching.
Third is the meaning of non-attainment within attainment;
others have the meaning of attainment.
Now, to clarify the meaning of non-attainment:
others hold that there is something existent that can be attained, and there is something nonexistent that can be attained.
If there were neither that which can be attained nor that which cannot be attained,
then there would be no two truths. Since the two truths do exist, [there must be both attainment and non-attainment].
Therefore, that which exists and does not exist can be called "attainment.
Now it is clarified:
existence does not abide in existence.
There is manifestation, yet it does not exist;
there is nothing to be apprehended.
There is no non-abiding in non-existence.
Non-manifestation (avijñapti) is not non-existent;
because there is no "non-existence" to be apprehended,
it is termed the meaning of "non-apprehension."
Because there is neither attainment nor non-attainment;
"existence" and "non-existence" are what we call the teaching.
Fourth, the principle of clarifying the internal and external is likewise so.
He was formerly outside the principles of the ultimate and the conventional;
now he is within the principles of the ultimate and the conventional. Because he is within these principles, [he is so designated].
This is what is called "teaching.
Fifth is the clarification of revelation and concealment:
the two truths of others are the principle of concealment.
Now, it is explained that these two truths are the opening of the teaching.
Why is this? Because there are those who abide in existence and those who abide in non-existence.
This concerns whether or not there are causes and conditions for the Tathāgata that are unobscured.
Now it is clarified that the two truths are the teaching:
that which is expressed exists, and that which is not expressed does not exist.
Where there is non-manifestation (avijñapti) but no existence,
the Tathāgata’s teaching immediately reveals it;
there is no obstruction or stagnation.
Therefore, a sutra says:
"For example, it is like the autumn moon situated in the sky, clearly revealed;
now it is likewise."
Therefore, there exists the teaching of "namelessness.
Sixth is the clarification of the meanings of the full and the partial:
in other schools, the two truths are considered partial.
Now it is clear that these two truths are complete. Why is this?
Because it possesses only duality and not non-duality, it contains only the teaching and lacks the underlying principle;
thus, it is called the "half-syllable."
Now, that which is clear and fully possesses both principle and teaching is called the "complete letter" (pūrṇākṣara).
For the time being, it is thus:
since he lacks the full [attainment],
he likewise lacks the half.
What is it that is half-full and half-empty? Since there is no "full," how can there be a "half"?
Master An said:
"To reduce it to the full is 'half';
to fulfill the half is 'full'."
Since there is no fullness, what could be diminished to become half?
Therefore, where there is no fullness, there is also no half.
Seventh, it clarifies that those who were ignorant of the two truths of others are now wise.
Why is this? The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"The wise regard clarity and ignorance as one; the foolish regard them as two."
The wise thoroughly comprehend that their nature is non-dual;
as it is with clarity and ignorance,
so it is with the ultimate and the conventional.
The identity of the two—ultimate and conventional—is for the ignorant;
their non-duality is for the wise.
This nature of non-duality is itself the true nature (*dharmatā*).
Thus we know that non-duality is the principle (li) and duality is the teaching (jiao).
Eighth, we now clarify essence and function (ti-yong).
That [other view] possesses only function but lacks substance;
since there is no substance, there is no function.
Now, however, it possesses both substance and function.
Ninth is clarifying the fundamental and the derivative:
non-duality is the fundamental;
duality is the derivative.
Since he has no root, how could there be any branches?
Now, both duality and non-duality are fully present.
Because they possess both the fundamental and the derivative,
it is said that the two truths are the teaching, while non-duality is the principle.
Tenth is the distinction between the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
Regarding the traditional explanation of the definitive (nītārtha) and the non-definitive (neyārtha):
it clarifies that the teachings of the Hīnayāna are non-definitive,
while the teachings of the Mahāyāna are definitive.
Within the Mahāyāna teachings, there are further two categories:
those such as the *Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* are considered of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*),
while the fifth, the teaching on the eternal abiding of *Nirvāṇa*, is considered of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Within the teachings of the five periods,
there are those that are definitive (nītārtha) and those that are non-definitive (neyārtha); such is the meaning of these two truths.
Is there a distinction between the definitive (nītārtha) and the non-definitive (neyārtha)?
The explanation states:
That [text] clarifies this.
If one takes the three provisional designations as the principle of the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and the fourfold forgetting as the principle of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya),
these two truths are exclusively of definitive meaning (nītārtha).
There is nothing that is not of provisional meaning.
Now it is clarified:
both of these two truths are [themselves] of provisional meaning.
Why is this? Although I speak of the two truths as existing,
my intention is to reveal that they do not exist.
To speak of non-desire reveals that it is not non-existent;
to speak of existence and non-existence reveals that it is neither existent nor non-existent—this is called the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Your position of abiding in existence does not indicate non-existence.
Non-abiding is neither non-manifestation nor not non-existent;
existence and non-existence are neither manifestation nor neither-existence-nor-non-existence.
These two non-manifestations are non-dual.
Because it cannot manifest the Path, it is not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Now, we shall clarify the existence or non-existence of causes and conditions.
Manifest form (vijñapti) is not existent; non-manifest form (avijñapti) is not non-existent.
Both existence and non-existence are employed to reveal the path of non-duality of purity.
Therefore, it is called "definitive meaning" (*nītārtha*). Thus, the Great Sūtra says:
"These two kinds of speech..."
It was for the sake of a single word;
now it is likewise:
the two—cause and condition—are presented to manifest non-duality.
These two causal conditions are for the purpose of awakening to non-duality;
the two serve as the gateway to the teaching.
One does not take these two statements as the definitive teaching.
However, in our school, there are not only teachings of definitive meaning (nītārtha),
but also those of non-definitive meaning (neyārtha).
It possesses both the definitive and the non-definitive meanings. Why?
Because it is simply a teaching gate consisting of the two truths.
There is a skillful means:
namely, hearing about the two yet not abiding in the two;
because of these two, one awakens to non-duality—this is called the definitive meaning (nītārtha).
Lacking skillful means,
one hears of duality in the second stage and yet does not realize non-duality; this is called the "unrealized meaning" (neyārtha).
Therefore, at this present time, both the definitive and the non-definitive meanings are fully extant.
Briefly, ten types have been clarified.
The principle for determining whether there is gain or loss in studying the two truths is as follows.
Furthermore, the ten types are:
first, the meaning of principle and teaching;
second, the characterized and the uncharacterized.
Third is attaining non-attainment;
fourth is the principle of the internal and external;
fifth is opening and covering.
Sixth, the partial and the complete;
seventh, the ignorant and the wise;
eighth, the essence and its function.
Ninth is the fundamental and the derivative;
tenth is the thorough and the incomplete, and so forth.
Next, there is a general summary and analysis.
It was previously stated that others possess only the teaching (śāsana) but lack the principle (yukti);
now, however, it is claimed they possess both principle and teaching. This is not the case.
As Kai-shan said: "The Two Truths are the ultimate destination of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā),
the supreme principle of the single reality and non-duality."
It is further said:
"Non-dual yet dual, the Middle Way is the Two Truths;
dual yet non-dual, the Two Truths are the Middle Way."
If that is so, since there are both dual and non-dual [teachings] regarding that principle and its scriptural authority,
why do you say it does not exist? Thus he challenges [the opponent].
Regarding your two truths:
are they a matter of ultimate principle,
or are they a matter of expedient means?
That clarity is the principle of the two truths. [Objection:
If these two are the principle, [then...]
There is then no principle of non-duality.
If there were a principle of non-duality,
it would constitute three principles.
You maintain that there are only two principles and no third;
therefore, there is no principle of the Middle Way as non-duality.
Now, let this be clarified.
The two truths are not the ultimate principle;
rather, they are a gateway of skillful means,
like the three chariots outside the gate.
Outside the gate there were actually no three vehicles;
it was through skillful means that he spoke of three,
so as to lead them to realize they are not three.
It is the same now:
in reality there are no two truths;
it is through skillful means that two are spoken of in order to lead one to realize non-duality.
Therefore, the two truths are the gateway of the teaching.
Furthermore, [the opponent] objects:
"You clarify that non-duality is the Middle Way."
Is the Middle Way situated outside the two truths,
or is it subsumed within them?
You must clarify this.
The two truths encompass all phenomena exhaustively.
In the ultimate truth, one transcends nirvana above and cuts off birth-and-death below;
thus, the four propositions are forgotten.
The hundred negations are thoroughly dispelled;
that all things are non-existent is the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya),
while that all phenomena are existent is the conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya).
Externally, there is no place where phenomena exist. If that is so, and there is only the principle of the two truths,
where could existence possibly be?
Furthermore, what is this thing that is neither existent nor non-existent?
That which is not existent is still non-existent;
that which is not non-existent is still existent.
Since there still exist [the views of] existence, non-existence, annihilation,
and permanence, how can one speak of the Middle Way?
For this reason, it is now clarified.
The two truths are the gateway of teaching;
non-duality is the Middle Way.
Furthermore, there is nothing that is not "other," and there is neither existence nor non-existence.
Now there is "being," "non-being," "neither being nor non-being," and "both being and non-being"—
this is the reversal [of the previous positions]. Others, however, maintain only the two principles of being and non-being.
There is no path of non-duality.
Now, there is only the path of non-duality, which is neither existence nor non-existence.
Question: Since there is neither existence nor non-existence, there should be no Two Truths.
The commentary states:
In reality, there is neither existence nor non-existence;
it is only for the sake of skillful means that one provisionally speaks of existence and non-existence.
The provisional use of "existence" and "non-existence" is for the purpose of awakening one to the fact that there is neither existence nor non-existence; it is for this reason.
The elucidation of the two truths is a pedagogical gateway;
yet, these two truths are not ultimately dual.
They are simply the one and the same truth studied by the practitioner.
There is gain and there is loss;
there is the perfected nature and the imagined nature, and so forth.
The Great Master has always used analogies such as the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*).
Those who possess skillful means will live long by taking it;
those without skillful means will meet an early death by taking it.
The nectar of immortality has never caused anyone to die prematurely through its cultivation.
The cultivation of the faculties arises from two conditions;
now it is likewise so—
there is only one or two truths.
Learning with skillful means constitutes the conventional;
learning without skillful means constitutes the ultimate nature.
Because there are skillful means, there is attainment.
To lack skillful means is a failure.

Regarding the two truths, there has never been a nature that is either real or provisional, nor a gain or loss that is real or provisional. There is no nature that is real or provisional, nor any gain or loss that is real or provisional.
It arises from two conditions;
yet even these self-nature and causal conditions are likewise not two.
Those with skillful means study the causal conditions for the nature of phenomena;
those without skillful means do not.
The nature of things is established through causes and conditions.
It is like one without skillful means who consumes nectar and it becomes poison,
while one with skillful means consumes that same poison and it becomes nectar.
It is the same for those who study the two truths:
those who lack skillful means study the dependent origination as having intrinsic nature,
whereas those who possess skillful means study intrinsic nature as being dependently originated.
For this reason,
in studying the two truths, there is both gain and loss;
there is intrinsic nature and there are causal conditions.
Question: Regarding that principle of the natural, innate nature established through the causes and conditions of training—should one grasp this principle or not grasp it?
Explanation:
There is both grasping and non-grasping.

According to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*,
he is collectively designated as a "manure remover.
